name: Security Operations
plainMeaning: This domain is about the daily work of keeping an organisation safe. It covers watching for trouble, handling incidents and disasters, and protecting data, equipment and people.

topics.name: Investigations and digital forensics
topics.simpleExplanation: When something bad happens on a computer, someone must find out what happened and prove it. That is an investigation. Digital forensics is the careful science of collecting computer evidence without changing it. Think of a crime scene in a house. You take photos first, you touch nothing without gloves, and you write down who handled each item. If you are careless, the proof is lost. A court may then refuse it. So care, order and good records matter most.

studyNotes.heading: Kinds of investigation and the proof each one needs
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the different kinds of investigation, because the kind of investigation decides how strong your proof must be.

Think of a quarrel at home about who broke a window. A parent only needs to be fairly sure before deciding who will pay. A court that could send somebody to prison must be far more certain. The higher the consequence, the stronger the proof must be.

There are five kinds to know.

- Administrative: inside the organisation, such as a staff matter or a system fault. The proof needed is low, and the aim is usually to find out what happened and put it right.
- Criminal: carried out by law enforcement because a law may have been broken. The standard is beyond a reasonable doubt, which is the highest one.
- Civil: one party sues another, usually for money. The standard is preponderance of the evidence, which means more likely true than not.
- Regulatory: a government body checks whether its rules were followed. The standard depends on that body.
- Industry standards: a contract or an industry group sets the rules, such as the rules for shops that accept payment cards.

Here is a workplace example. A bank notices that a member of staff has been looking at customer accounts for no good reason. It begins as an administrative matter. Then the team finds that money has been moved. Now it may be criminal. So the way evidence was handled in the very first hour suddenly matters a great deal.

This gives us the manager's rule. If a case might reach a court, involve the legal team early, and treat everything as evidence from the start. You cannot go back later and collect it properly.

Also decide early whether to call law enforcement. That decision belongs to senior management, with legal advice. It is not for a technician acting alone. Calling the police can bring publicity, and they may take equipment away, so the business needs to weigh that.

Here is what to take away. The kind of investigation sets the standard of proof, criminal is the highest, and legal advice comes early.

studyNotes.heading: Evidence: what kinds exist and what a court will accept
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at evidence itself. We will cover the kinds of evidence, and what makes a court willing to accept it.

Imagine that you are telling a friend that your neighbour's dog dug up your garden. A muddy paw print is something you can point to. A photo is a record. Your neighbour saying that she saw it happen is a statement. Courts sort evidence in much the same way.

- Real evidence is a physical thing, such as a hard drive or a laptop.
- Documentary evidence is written or recorded information, such as logs, emails and contracts.
- Testimonial evidence is what a witness says under oath.
- Demonstrative evidence helps explain other evidence, such as a chart or a timeline.

Evidence must be admissible, which means that a court will accept it. There are three tests. It must be relevant, meaning it helps to prove a fact. It must be material, meaning that fact matters in this case. It must be competent, meaning it was collected legally and reliably.

Two older rules also appear on the exam. The best evidence rule prefers the original document over a copy. The parol evidence rule says that when an agreement has been put in writing, the written version is taken as the whole agreement.

The hearsay rule limits second-hand statements. A person cannot normally repeat what somebody else said as proof that it was true. Computer logs could fall under this rule, because a machine cannot be questioned. But there is an exception for business records. If logs are made routinely, as a normal part of the business, and someone can explain how the system works, they can usually be accepted.

Here is a workplace example. A company wants to rely on its door access logs in court. It shows that the logs are created automatically every day, that nobody can change them, and that the security manager can explain the system. That makes them far easier to accept.

Good evidence should also be authentic, accurate, complete and convincing.

Here is your takeaway. Know real, documentary, testimonial and demonstrative evidence, and remember that admissible means relevant, material and competent.

studyNotes.heading: Chain of custody
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at chain of custody, which is one of the most important ideas in this topic.

Chain of custody is a written record of who held the evidence, when, where and why, from the moment it was collected until it reaches the court. Think of tracking a parcel. Every time the parcel changes hands, a scan is recorded. If the parcel disappears for two days and turns up again, you would wonder what happened to it.

Each entry in the record should show these things.

- What the item is, with its description and serial number.
- Who collected it, and from where.
- The date and time of collection and of every transfer.
- Who released it and who received it, with signatures.
- Why it was moved.
- Where and how it was stored.
- The hash value, if it is a digital item. A hash is a digital fingerprint, and if the data changes, the hash changes.

The evidence must stay under control the whole time. It should be sealed in a tamper-evident bag, which shows clearly if anyone has opened it. It should be labelled and kept in a locked store with limited access. Each person who touches it signs the log.

Here is a workplace example. An investigator seizes a laptop on Monday morning, and records its serial number and the time. She seals it and hands it to the evidence custodian, and both of them sign. On Tuesday, a forensic examiner signs it out, makes a copy, and signs it back in. Anyone reading that record can account for every minute.

Now change the story. Suppose the laptop sat on an open desk over lunch, and nobody wrote that down. The defence can argue that somebody could have altered it. One gap can make the evidence useless, even if nothing really happened to it.

Notice that the chain of custody does not prove that the evidence is true. It proves that the evidence has been controlled.

Here is what to take away. Record who, what, when, where and why for every hand-over, and leave no gaps.

studyNotes.heading: The order of volatility, with a worked example
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at the order in which digital evidence should be collected.

Volatile means something that disappears quickly. Think of a detective at a beach. Footprints near the waves must be photographed first, because the tide is coming. The carved initials on the rock can wait. So we collect the most short-lived evidence first. The accepted order comes from an internet guidance document called RFC 3227. RFC stands for Request for Comments.

Learn this exact order, from most volatile to least.

- Central processing unit registers and cache. The central processing unit, or CPU, is the chip that does the computer's work.
- Routing table, ARP cache, process table, kernel statistics and main memory.
- Temporary file systems.
- Disk.
- Remote logging and monitoring data.
- Physical configuration and network topology.
- Archival media, such as backup tapes.

Let us explain the new words. The routing table tells a computer where to send network traffic. ARP stands for Address Resolution Protocol, and its cache matches network addresses to devices. The process table lists the programs that are running. The kernel is the core of the operating system. Network topology means how the network is laid out.

Now a worked example. An investigator arrives at a server that is still running, and that may have been used to steal data.

Step one, she photographs the screen and the room. Registers and cache change too fast to capture separately in most cases, so step two, she captures memory, using a trusted tool. That brings in the routing table, running processes and network connections as well. Step three, she copies temporary files if they will not survive. Step four, she makes a full copy of the disk. Step five, she requests the logs held on the central log server. Step six, she records how the machine was connected. Step seven, she collects any backup tapes.

A common trap is to shut the machine down first. Pulling the plug destroys everything in memory, including encryption keys and running malware. Do not power off before you have decided what you are willing to lose.

Here is your takeaway. Collect what will vanish first, so memory comes before disk, and disk comes before backup tapes.

studyNotes.heading: Forensic tools, tactics and procedures
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how digital forensics is actually done, including the tools and the working steps.

Digital forensics is the careful science of collecting and examining computer evidence so that it stands up in court. Think of a doctor taking a blood sample. The sample is labelled and stored carefully, and the tests are run on portions of it, so that the original stays available.

These are the main tools.

A write blocker is a device that lets you read a disk, but stops any change to it. Imaging software makes a bit-for-bit copy, also called a forensic image, including deleted areas of the disk. A hash tool calculates the digital fingerprint, often with SHA-256, which stands for Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit result. Memory capture tools record what is in the main memory. A packet capture tool records network traffic. A Faraday bag is a pouch that blocks radio signals, so a seized phone cannot be wiped remotely.

Here is the usual procedure. It is a set of steps, but practitioners may adjust the detail to the case.

- Identify what may hold evidence.
- Preserve it, so it cannot change.
- Collect it, in order of volatility.
- Examine the copy for relevant data.
- Analyse what it means.
- Present the findings.

The golden rule is to work on a verified copy, and to protect the original. Make the image, hash the original, hash the image, and compare. If the two fingerprints match, the copy is exact.

The main tactics include building a timeline of events, recovering deleted files, and looking at slack space, which is the unused end of a storage block where old data can remain. Examiners also compare the clocks of different systems, because logs in different time zones can seem out of order.

Here is a workplace example. A company suspects that a contractor copied designs to a USB stick, a small plug-in storage device. The examiner images the contractor's laptop through a write blocker, verifies the hashes, and searches the copy. She finds a record of the USB stick being connected at the time of the theft.

Here is what to take away. Protect the original, work on a verified copy, and record every step.

studyNotes.heading: Investigative techniques, artifacts and the report
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at the techniques investigators use, the traces they look for, and how the work is written up.

An interview is a conversation that gathers facts from someone willing to help. An interrogation questions a suspect. It carries legal risk, so leave it to trained staff or to the police.

Investigators often think about MOM, which stands for motive, opportunity and means. Motive is why a person did it. Opportunity is the chance to do it. Means is the ability to do it. Locard's exchange principle says that a criminal always leaves something behind and takes something away. Think of a burglar who leaves a footprint and carries off some mud on a shoe. Computers work the same way.

Enticement leaves a lure for someone already planning harm, and it is legal. Entrapment persuades someone to commit a crime they did not plan, and it is illegal.

Artifacts are the traces left behind. The outline names four places to look.

- Data: files and their metadata, which is data about data, such as the date a file was created.
- Computer: deleted files, browser history, memory and system settings.
- Network: traffic captures, firewall logs and records of connections.
- Mobile device: call logs, messages, location history and app data.

The report is where the work becomes useful. It states the facts, the tools used, the steps taken and the times. It avoids guesses and opinions on guilt. Another expert should be able to repeat the work and reach the same result. Write it clearly enough for a judge or a manager who is not technical.

Here is a workplace example. A weak report says that the employee obviously stole the files. A strong report says that at a stated time, the account named in the log copied 300 files to an external drive with a stated serial number. The second report shows what happened, and leaves the conclusion to the people who are entitled to decide.

Keep the documents secure as well, and share them only with those who need them.

Here is your takeaway. Know motive, opportunity and means, know the four artifact types, and report only facts that another expert could repeat.

topics.memoryHook: Think of a crime scene: photo first, gloves on, write down every hand that touches the item.

question.prompt: An investigator arrives at a running laptop that is suspected of being used for fraud. Which item should the investigator collect FIRST?
options: A full image of the hard drive
Printed papers on the desk
The contents of main memory
Backup tapes kept in the office safe
question.explanation: Memory is lost when power goes, so it comes first under the order of volatility. The hard drive image is tempting, but disk data lasts far longer than memory, so it can wait.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An investigator is collecting evidence from a running server. Time is short. Which of these should be collected FIRST?
options: Temporary files on the server
The routing table and the list of running processes
A complete bit-for-bit image of the server's main disk
The offsite backup tapes for that server
practiceQuestions.explanation: The routing table and process table sit near the top of the order of volatility. Temporary files are tempting because they also change quickly, but they come after memory and related data.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A seized hard drive was left unattended on an examiner's desk for two hours, and nothing was recorded. The drive and its hash are unchanged. What is the MOST serious concern for a later court case?
options: The drive may have become slower
The examiner should have used a different hashing tool
The disk image may be too large to present
There is a gap in the chain of custody
practiceQuestions.explanation: An unrecorded period out of control is a gap in the chain of custody, and it can be challenged in court. Changing the hashing tool is tempting, but the method was not the problem. Control of the item was.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An examiner has made a forensic image of a disk. Which step BEST shows that the image is an exact copy of the original?
options: Compare the hash of the image with the hash of the original
Compare the file sizes of the image and the disk
Open a sample of the files and read them
Ask a second examiner to review and sign the chain of custody form
practiceQuestions.explanation: Matching hashes show that the two are identical, bit for bit. Comparing sizes is tempting, but two sets of data can be the same size and still differ.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A software company sues a former partner for misusing its code. Which standard of proof will the court MOST likely apply?
options: Beyond a reasonable doubt
Whatever standard the company's own policy sets
Preponderance of the evidence
Absolute certainty
practiceQuestions.explanation: A civil case between two parties uses preponderance of the evidence, meaning more likely true than not. Beyond a reasonable doubt is tempting because it is the best-known standard, but it applies to criminal cases.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants to use its server logs in court, but the other side argues that the logs are hearsay. Which fact would BEST help the company?
options: The logs are created routinely as a normal part of the business
The logs were printed on company letterhead
The logs were stored for longer than the law requires
The logs were carefully checked and summarised by a senior manager
practiceQuestions.explanation: Records made routinely in the normal course of business can fall under the business records exception. A summary by a manager is tempting, but it adds another layer of second-hand statement.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Investigators seize a smartphone that is switched on. They are concerned that the suspect could erase it remotely. What should they do FIRST?
options: Remove the battery and throw away the SIM card
Browse the phone quickly to find the key messages
Ask the mobile network to send a software update
Place it in a Faraday bag and keep it powered
practiceQuestions.explanation: A Faraday bag blocks signals, so a remote wipe cannot arrive, and keeping power preserves volatile data. Browsing the phone is tempting, but it changes the evidence.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A manager suspects an employee of fraud and wants to confront the employee at once in a closed room. What should the security professional advise?
options: Record the confrontation secretly so that it can be used later
Leave any questioning of a suspect to trained staff or the police
Hold the meeting straight away, before the employee can hide evidence
Ask the employee's colleagues to question the employee informally
practiceQuestions.explanation: Questioning a suspect is an interrogation, which carries legal risk and needs trained people. Acting at once feels decisive, but an unskilled confrontation can spoil the case.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An examiner finds a tool left on a server by an intruder and also finds that customer files were copied away. Which idea does this finding BEST illustrate?
options: The best evidence rule
The order of volatility
Locard's exchange principle
The parol evidence rule
practiceQuestions.explanation: Locard's principle says that an intruder leaves something behind and takes something away. The best evidence rule is tempting because this is evidence, but that rule is about preferring originals.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which statement BEST belongs in a forensic report that may be read in court?
options: At the logged time, this account copied 300 files to the listed drive
The employee clearly intended to harm the company
In my experience, staff with money problems are likely to steal
The suspect probably deleted more files that we could not find
practiceQuestions.explanation: A report states facts that another expert could check and repeat. Comments on intent can sound convincing, but they are opinions on matters the examiner cannot show.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An examiner builds a timeline from three systems, and the events appear to be out of order. The servers are in different countries. What should the examiner do FIRST?
options: Remove the events that do not fit the expected pattern
Use only the logs from the most important server
Record each system's clock setting and convert the times to one standard
Ask administrators to reset the clocks on the three servers now
practiceQuestions.explanation: Recording each clock setting and converting to a common time puts events in true order without changing evidence. Resetting the clocks sounds helpful, but it alters the systems and does not explain earlier records.

topics.name: Logging and monitoring
topics.simpleExplanation: Logging means writing down what happens on your systems. Monitoring means watching those records for trouble. Think of a shop with cameras, a visitor book and a guard who checks them. Tools can watch traffic, collect records in one place and even react by themselves. But tools need care. Too many false alarms and people stop looking. Good monitoring means the right records are kept safe, the alarms are tuned, and someone actually looks and acts on what they see.

studyNotes.heading: Intrusion detection and prevention
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the tools that watch for attacks and the tools that can stop them.

An IDS, or intrusion detection system, watches and raises an alarm. An IPS, or intrusion prevention system, sits in the path of the traffic and can block it. Together they are often called IDPS. Think of a smoke alarm compared with a sprinkler. The alarm tells you about the fire. The sprinkler does something about it.

Because an IPS sits in the path, it is called inline. An IDS usually receives a copy of the traffic, so it is called passive. That difference matters. If an IPS fails or blocks the wrong thing, real work can stop.

Both tools come in two kinds. Network-based tools watch traffic on a part of the network. Host-based tools run on one computer, and can see what happens on it, including activity hidden by encryption while travelling over the network. Encryption is the scrambling of data so that only key holders can read it.

They find trouble in two main ways.

Signature-based detection matches known attack patterns. It is accurate for known attacks, but it misses new ones. Anomaly-based detection, also called behaviour-based, learns what is normal and flags what is different. It can catch new attacks, but it gives more false alarms.

There are four possible results, and you should know each one. A true positive is a real attack with an alarm. A true negative is normal activity with no alarm. A false positive is an alarm with no real attack. A false negative is a real attack with no alarm. The false negative is usually the worst, because nobody knows anything is wrong.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital puts an IPS in front of its public web servers, where blocking attacks quickly matters. It puts an IDS on the network that connects medical devices, because a wrongly blocked signal there could harm a patient.

Here is what to take away. An IDS alerts and an IPS blocks, signatures miss new attacks, and a false negative is the most dangerous result.

studyNotes.heading: SIEM and SOAR
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the systems that pull all the alerts together, and at the systems that act on them.

SIEM stands for security information and event management. It collects logs from many systems into one place. It puts them in a common format, which is called normalising. Then it links events together, which is called correlation, and it raises alerts.

Think of a shop manager who hears three separate things. A customer says that a door was left open. A cashier says that a stranger asked about the safe. A cleaner says that the alarm box looks damaged. Each report seems small. Together they tell a story. A SIEM does the same with logs.

Here is a workplace example. One failed login means little. Fifty failed logins, then a success, then a large download from the same account, tells a very different story. A SIEM can spot that pattern across the login server, the file server and the firewall, even though no single system saw all of it.

A SIEM also provides dashboards, which are live summary screens, and it keeps logs that help with investigations and with proving compliance. Compliance means showing that you are following the rules.

SOAR stands for security orchestration, automation and response. Where a SIEM finds and tells, SOAR does. It follows playbooks, which are written steps for a type of event. For example, when a phishing email is reported, SOAR can pull the same email from every mailbox, block the sender and open a ticket. Phishing is a trick message that fools people into giving something away.

Automation brings speed. It also brings risk. A poorly written playbook could disable the account of the chief executive during a busy day. So playbooks are tested, and high-impact actions often wait for a person to approve them.

A SIEM is only as good as what you feed into it, and only useful if someone responds. A manager must make sure that staff have time and clear responsibility for working through the alerts. A tool that nobody watches gives a false sense of safety.

Here is your takeaway. A SIEM collects, links and alerts, while SOAR follows playbooks and acts on what is found.

studyNotes.heading: Continuous monitoring and tuning
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at continuous monitoring, and at tuning, which keeps the alerts useful.

Continuous monitoring means checking security all the time, and not once a year. Think of your health. A yearly check-up is useful, but a heart monitor that runs all day can catch a problem the moment it starts. In the workplace, continuous monitoring keeps watch on controls, threats and vulnerabilities, so that decisions are based on the current state of things.

Tuning means adjusting detection rules to fit your own environment, so that real alarms stand out. Every organisation is different. A backup server that sends huge files every night is perfectly normal. The same behaviour from a reception computer is not.

Imagine a car alarm that goes off whenever a leaf lands on the car. Very soon, everybody on the street ignores it. Security teams suffer from this too, and it is called alert fatigue. When staff are flooded with alarms, they stop looking, and the real one gets missed.

Worked example. Let us walk through tuning a noisy rule.

Step one, the team notices that one rule produces 800 alerts a day. Step two, they study a sample of those alerts, and find that 790 of them come from the company's own vulnerability scanner. Step three, they confirm that the scanner's address is really the scanner. Step four, they write a narrow exception for that one address and that one rule. Step five, they test the change through the normal approval process. Step six, they measure the result, which is now about 10 alerts a day, and each of those deserves a look. Step seven, they review the exception on a regular basis, because an attacker could one day abuse that address.

Notice what the team did not do. They did not simply switch off the rule, because then a real attack would go unnoticed. They fixed the cause of the noise.

A manager might also track measures such as the time taken to detect an event and the time taken to respond.

Here is what to take away. Monitor all the time, and when a tool is noisy, tune it carefully and do not turn it off.

studyNotes.heading: Log management
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at how logs are handled, so that people can trust them.

A log is a record of events on a system. Think of a visitor book at a front desk. It is only useful if the pages are not torn out, the times are correct, and somebody reads it now and then.

These are the main practices to remember.

Centralise the logs. Send them to a separate server, so that an attacker who takes over one system cannot easily erase the record of what was done.

Protect them. Limit who can read them, and limit who can change them even more strictly. Some systems use WORM storage, which stands for write once, read many. Once written, the data cannot be altered. Hashing log files, which means taking a digital fingerprint of them, shows whether they have been changed.

Synchronise the clocks. NTP, or Network Time Protocol, keeps all systems on the same time. Without it, events from different systems cannot be put into the right order, and evidence can be challenged.

Keep the right things. Log successful and failed logins, changes to privileged accounts, changes to settings, and access to sensitive data. Do not log passwords or other secrets.

Keep them for the right time. Retention means how long you hold on to records. Policy, law and contracts set the period. Too short, and you cannot investigate. Too long, and you pay to store risk that you did not need to keep.

Review them regularly. Automated tools do much of this. A clipping level is a set limit below which events are not reported, such as five failed logins. This reduces noise, so that repeated failures stand out. Sampling means reviewing a portion of the logs, to draw a conclusion about all of them.

Here is a workplace example. An attacker gets administrator access to a web server and deletes its local logs. The company's central log server already holds a copy, so the investigators can still see what happened.

The manager's view is that logging supports accountability, which means being able to tie an action to one person.

Here is your takeaway. Logs must be central, protected, time-synchronised, kept for the right period and actually reviewed.

studyNotes.heading: Egress monitoring
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at egress monitoring, which means watching what leaves your network.

Egress means going out. Ingress means coming in. Many teams concentrate on keeping attackers out, and forget to watch what is leaving. Think of a shop. There are guards at the entrance to greet customers, and security tags that sound an alarm at the exit if someone walks out with goods that were not paid for. Egress monitoring is the alarm at the exit.

The main tool is DLP, or data loss prevention. A DLP tool looks for sensitive data, such as card numbers or customer records, in emails, uploads and files copied to removable drives.

There are two main kinds. Network-based DLP inspects data moving through the network. Endpoint-based DLP runs on the user's computer, and can see copying to a USB stick, which is a small plug-in storage device. To work well, DLP depends on data being classified and labelled, so that the tool knows what matters.

The outline also expects you to know these related ideas.

A watermark is a hidden or visible mark placed in a file, which helps to trace where a leaked copy came from. Steganography hides data inside a harmless file, such as a photo, so that it is hard to spot. An attacker might use it to carry stolen data out. Encrypted traffic is another challenge, because a DLP tool cannot read what it cannot decrypt. Some organisations therefore inspect encrypted web traffic at a controlled point, and they tell their staff about this in policy.

Egress rules on firewalls also help. Malware often needs to call back to the attacker. A server that has no reason to reach the internet should not be allowed to.

Here is a workplace example. A staff member tries to email a spreadsheet of customer details to a personal account. The DLP system spots a pattern of national identity numbers, blocks the message, and alerts the security team. The team treats it first as a possible mistake, and then checks the facts.

A manager would also ask about privacy, and make sure that staff are told that monitoring takes place.

Here is what to take away. Watch what leaves, classify data so that tools can recognise it, and tell staff that monitoring happens.

studyNotes.heading: Threat intelligence, threat hunting and UEBA
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at how to learn about attackers, how to search for them, and how to spot unusual behaviour.

Threat intelligence is useful knowledge about attackers and their methods. Threat feeds deliver it as a steady stream, such as lists of bad internet addresses and file fingerprints. These are known as indicators of compromise, which means the signs that an attack has taken place. Standard formats help tools to share this. STIX, or Structured Threat Information Expression, describes threats, and TAXII, or Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information, carries them between organisations.

Threat hunting is a person actively searching for attackers who have already got past the defences. It assumes that a breach may have happened, and it does not wait for an alert. Think of a neighbourhood watch that walks the streets looking for anything out of place, instead of waiting for a burglar alarm to ring.

Hunters often describe attackers using two models. The cyber kill chain sets out seven stages, in this order.

- Reconnaissance, which is gathering information.
- Weaponisation, which is preparing the attack.
- Delivery.
- Exploitation.
- Installation.
- Command and control.
- Actions on objectives.

The other model is called ATT and CK, from an organisation named MITRE. It is a large catalogue of the tactics and techniques that real attackers use.

UEBA stands for user and entity behaviour analytics. An entity is something other than a person, such as a server or a device. UEBA learns normal behaviour for each user and entity, and then flags what is unusual. A clerk who suddenly downloads thousands of files at two in the morning stands out, even if the account has every right to read those files. UEBA is especially good at finding insider threats and stolen accounts.

Here is a workplace example. A feed reports a new attack method used against banks. A hunter at a bank searches its logs for signs of that method and finds one server contacting an unknown address. UEBA also shows that an administrator account is behaving strangely. Together they reveal an intruder that no alarm had caught.

Here is your takeaway. Intelligence informs you, hunting assumes a breach, and UEBA compares behaviour with what is normal.

SIEM finds and tells, while SOAR acts.
Tune noisy tools rather than switching them off.

question.prompt: A security team receives hundreds of alerts each day from its intrusion detection system. Most are false alarms, and staff have started to ignore them. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Review the alerts and tune the rules to fit the environment
Turn off the rules that create the most alerts
Hire more analysts to read every alert
Replace the system with an intrusion prevention system
question.explanation: Tuning fixes the cause, so real alarms stand out. Turning off noisy rules is tempting, but it may also hide real attacks and create false negatives.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A factory wants to detect attacks on the network that controls its production machines. A wrongly blocked command could stop the production line. Which tool is BEST?
options: An inline intrusion prevention system on that network
An anti-malware scanner on the office computers
A passive network intrusion detection system
A web application firewall on the company website
practiceQuestions.explanation: A passive detection system watches a copy of the traffic, so it cannot block a command by mistake. An inline prevention system is tempting because it can stop attacks, but a false block could halt production.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A new type of attack has appeared, and no security vendor has published a pattern for it yet. Which detection method has the BEST chance of noticing it?
options: Anomaly-based detection
Signature-based detection
A deny list of known bad files
A clipping level on failed logins
practiceQuestions.explanation: Anomaly-based detection flags what differs from normal, so it can notice something never seen before. Signature-based detection is tempting because it is accurate, but it can only match attacks that are already known.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's intrusion detection system saw an attack pass by but raised no alarm. The breach was found three months later. What was the detection result at the time of the attack?
options: True negative
False positive
True positive
False negative
practiceQuestions.explanation: A real attack with no alarm is a false negative. False positive is the commonly confused term, but that is an alarm when no real attack took place.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An analyst needs to see failed logins, a firewall event and a large file transfer linked together as one possible attack. Which tool is designed to do this?
options: A vulnerability scanner
A security information and event management system
A data loss prevention tool
A host-based firewall
practiceQuestions.explanation: A SIEM collects logs from many sources and correlates them. A data loss prevention tool is tempting because of the file transfer, but it looks at data leaving and does not link events across systems.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker took control of a server and removed the evidence from its local event log. Which earlier practice would BEST have preserved a record of the attacker's actions?
options: Setting a higher clipping level
Turning on the local firewall
Keeping the local logs for a longer period
Sending logs to a separate central server
practiceQuestions.explanation: A central log server keeps a copy that the attacker cannot easily reach. Keeping local logs for longer is tempting, but the attacker can still delete them on the compromised machine.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Investigators cannot work out the order of events because timestamps from two servers do not agree. Which control would have BEST prevented this problem?
options: Network Time Protocol on all systems
Write once, read many storage
A longer log retention period
Encrypting the log files
practiceQuestions.explanation: Network Time Protocol keeps every system on the same time, so events can be placed in order. Write once storage is tempting because it protects logs, but it protects them from change, not from having the wrong time.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security team suspects that an insider is hiding company data inside ordinary holiday photos and emailing them out. Which technique does this describe?
options: Watermarking
Tokenisation
Steganography
Hashing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Steganography hides data inside another harmless file. Watermarking is tempting because it also places something in a file, but it marks a file in order to trace it and does not carry hidden data out.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security team spends part of each week searching its logs for attackers, even though no alert has fired. Which activity is this?
options: Vulnerability scanning
Threat hunting
Log rotation
Tuning
practiceQuestions.explanation: Threat hunting actively searches for attackers on the assumption that one may already be inside. Vulnerability scanning is tempting because it is also proactive, but it looks for weaknesses and not for attackers.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A clerk's account has valid access to payroll files, but it suddenly reads thousands of them late at night. No rule has been broken. Which tool is MOST likely to flag this?
options: A static packet filter
A signature-based intrusion detection system
A disk encryption product
User and entity behaviour analytics
practiceQuestions.explanation: Behaviour analytics compares activity with what is normal for that account. A signature-based system is tempting because it raises alerts, but this is valid access with no known attack pattern to match.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security manager is planning a system that will automatically remove a reported phishing email from every mailbox and open a ticket. Which capability is the manager planning?
options: Security orchestration, automation and response
A central log server
A threat intelligence feed
A host-based intrusion detection system
practiceQuestions.explanation: SOAR follows playbooks to act automatically on events. A threat intelligence feed is tempting because it relates to phishing information, but a feed only supplies information and takes no action.

topics.name: Configuration management
topics.simpleExplanation: Configuration management keeps every computer set up the way you approved. Think of a school where every classroom is arranged to the same plan. Provisioning means setting up a new system safely. A baseline is the approved setup that you measure against. Automation lets tools build and check systems the same way every time. When a system drifts away from its baseline, you notice it and put it back. Good configuration means fewer weak spots and fewer surprises for everyone.

studyNotes.heading: What configuration management does
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what configuration management is and why it matters.

Configuration management, often shortened to CM, makes sure that systems are set up in a known, approved and recorded way. Think of a school where every classroom follows the same plan. The desks are in the same places, and the fire notice is on the same wall. If a teacher walks into any room, there are no surprises. And if a room looks different from the plan, somebody notices.

CM answers three simple questions. What do we own? How is each thing set up? Has anything moved away from the approved setup?

Each thing that you track is called a configuration item. Servers, routers, software versions and even settings are all configuration items. Routers are the devices that pass network traffic between networks. The details of each item are kept in a CMDB, or configuration management database, which is the central record of them.

Why does a security manager care? There are several good reasons. Most attacks use weaknesses that are already known, such as a default password or an unnecessary service left running. Configuration management closes those weaknesses in a consistent way. It also helps during an incident, because you can compare a suspicious machine against how it should look. And it speeds up recovery, because you have a record of how to rebuild it.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital has 400 servers. A new attack targets one version of a piece of software. Because the hospital keeps a good CMDB, it can find every affected server within minutes, instead of checking each one by hand.

Now we need to clear up a common confusion. Configuration management and change management are partners, but they are different. Change management decides whether a change may happen. Configuration management records and checks the state of systems. One is the permission. The other is the record of how things actually stand.

The outline names three activities under this objective: provisioning, baselining and automation. We will take each of those in turn.

Here is what to take away. Configuration management keeps systems known, approved and recorded, and it works hand in hand with change management.

studyNotes.heading: Provisioning
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at provisioning, which is the first of the three activities that the outline names.

Provisioning means preparing and delivering a new system, so that it is ready and secure from its first day. Think of a new employee's first day. A good company has the desk, the badge and the training ready, and has already decided what that person may do. A poor company leaves the person to sort it out, and mistakes follow.

A safe provisioning process does these things.

First, it starts from an approved, hardened image. Hardening means removing what is not needed and closing weak settings. A golden image is the approved master copy, from which new systems are built.

Second, it applies current patches before the system goes live. A patch is a software fix from the maker.

Third, it removes default accounts and changes default passwords. Attackers keep lists of these passwords.

Fourth, it turns off unused services and ports. A port is a numbered doorway through which network traffic reaches a program. Every open doorway that nobody uses is a door that somebody could try.

Fifth, it records the new system in the inventory and the CMDB, or configuration management database.

The timing of this matters. A system connected to a network before it is hardened may be attacked within minutes. So build it in a protected area, and connect it only when it is ready.

Here is a workplace example. A bank needs twenty new virtual servers. A virtual server is a software-based computer that runs on shared hardware. The team builds them from the golden image, which already has the current patches and the correct settings. The tool records each one in the database automatically. A scan confirms that they match the standard before any of them handles real work.

Provisioning also covers cloud services, where a few clicks can create a new server in seconds. That ease brings risk. Someone may build a system that nobody records and nobody patches. This is often called shadow IT, meaning technology that is used without the knowledge of the technology team.

Here is your takeaway. Build new systems from a hardened image, patch them, remove defaults, close what is unused, and record them.

studyNotes.heading: Baselining
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at baselining, which gives you something to compare against.

A baseline is an approved snapshot of how a system should be set up. Think of a recipe. If the cake tastes strange, you can check what went into it against what the recipe says. Without the recipe, you are only guessing.

You do not need to invent a baseline from nothing. Published guides help you to build one. Examples are the benchmarks from CIS, the Center for Internet Security, and the technical guides from the United States Department of Defense, which are called STIGs, or Security Technical Implementation Guides.

You pick a guide, and then adjust it to your own needs. Adjusting it is called tailoring. Scoping means deciding which parts of the guide apply at all. A setting that is sensible for a public web server may be pointless for an isolated laboratory machine.

Different kinds of system will have different baselines. A database server, a laptop and a network switch each need their own. A switch is a device that connects computers within a network.

Drift is when a system slowly moves away from its baseline, often through small manual fixes. A technician makes a quick change during a busy night and forgets to record it. Then another technician does the same. Drift matters because every unrecorded change can open a weakness, and can also make recovery harder.

A baseline must be kept up to date. When a change is approved, update the baseline too, or the next new system will repeat the old weakness. Baselines themselves are placed under version control, so you always know which edition applied at which time.

Here is a workplace example. A government agency adopts a published benchmark for its laptops. It finds that one setting would break a piece of essential software. Instead of ignoring the matter, the agency records a formal exception, notes the reason, and adds another control in its place. A senior person approves that exception.

The manager's point of view here is about evidence. A documented baseline lets you show an auditor exactly what your standard is, and how well you follow it.

Here is what to take away. A baseline is the approved standard, you tailor it to your needs, and you keep it up to date.

studyNotes.heading: Automation
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at automation, which is the third activity that the outline names.

People make mistakes when they repeat a task a hundred times. Tools do not get tired. Think of a bakery. A baker who shapes every loaf by hand will make some larger than others. A machine set to the right weight will make them all the same.

Automation builds systems the same way every time, checks them against the baseline, and can correct drift. Drift means a system slowly moving away from its approved setup.

Here are the words that you should know.

IaC, or infrastructure as code, means writing the setup of systems in files, as if it were a program. Those files can be reviewed, tested, reused and version-controlled. Version control is a system that keeps every earlier edition of a file and records who changed what.

Configuration management tools apply the desired settings to many machines at once. Well-known examples are Ansible, Puppet and Chef. You describe how the system should look, and the tool makes it so.

Immutable infrastructure means that servers are never changed after they are built. If something needs to change, you build a new server and throw away the old one. Immutable simply means unable to be changed. This removes the possibility of drift.

Automation has clear security benefits. It provides speed, consistency and a record of what was done. A central set of files also makes it possible to fix a mistake once, and have the fix reach every system.

Automation also has a clear risk. One bad setting can spread to every system within minutes. Think again about the bakery machine. If it is set wrongly, every loaf that day is wrong. So automated changes still need review and testing, and they still go through change management. The files themselves need strong protection, because anyone who can alter them can alter every system, and secrets such as passwords must never be stored inside them.

Here is a workplace example. A retailer stores its server setup in version-controlled files. Two engineers must review any change. The change is tested on a small group of servers first, and only then does it go to all of them.

Here is your takeaway. Automation gives consistency and speed, but it can spread mistakes quickly, so it needs review and control.

studyNotes.heading: Keeping configuration under control every day
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at how configuration management works in daily life, and how it connects to other parts of security.

A configuration that was correct last year may not be correct today. Think of a garden. Planting it well once is not enough. You must keep checking it, and you must pull out the weeds as they appear.

There are several routine activities to understand.

Configuration auditing means comparing what is really running against what the records say should be running. It catches unapproved changes. It also catches errors in the records themselves.

Configuration status accounting means keeping track of the current state of each item, and of its history. In plain words, it tells you what version something is at, and how it got there.

Inventory is the foundation of it all. You cannot protect something if you do not know that it exists. Tools can discover devices on a network and compare them against the database. An unknown device may be harmless, or it may be a rogue device placed there by an attacker. Rogue means unauthorised.

Configuration management also strengthens other activities that you are studying in this domain. Patch management needs to know what is installed. Incident response needs to know what normal looks like. Disaster recovery needs enough detail to rebuild a system. Vulnerability scanning needs a list of what to scan.

Here is a workplace example. A university runs a monthly report comparing its database of assets with what its network tools can actually see. Last month, the report showed twelve computers that were not in the database. Ten were new laboratory machines that nobody had recorded. Two were personal devices that a contractor had connected. The university fixed its process for new machines, and it removed the two personal devices.

Notice the management thinking in that example. The team did not only fix the twelve machines. It also fixed the process that allowed those machines to go unrecorded. That is the idea of fixing the cause.

Good configuration management also needs ownership. Somebody must be responsible for each baseline and each database record, or else the records will quietly go out of date.

Here is what to take away. Audit what is really running, keep the inventory accurate, and fix the process as well as the single problem.

studyNotes.heading: Worked example: a drifting web server
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will walk through one complete example, so that you can see how the pieces fit together.

Think of a rental flat. The landlord has a written list of what should be in each room. Between tenants, someone walks through with the list. If a door lock has been changed without permission, the list makes this easy to see.

Now let us do the same thing with a company's web server.

Step one. The approved baseline says that the web server must not run file sharing, because it faces the internet and nobody needs that service on it.

Step two. An automated weekly check compares the server against the baseline, and it finds that file sharing has been switched on.

Step three. The tool raises an alert and records the difference, including the date on which it first appeared.

Step four. The team checks the change records, looking for an approved change. There is none. That makes this an unauthorised change.

Step five. The team considers whether this might be an attack. They review the logs, and they find that a technician switched the service on to copy a large file, and then forgot about it. So this is a mistake, not an intruder. Had the logs shown an unknown account, the team would have treated it as an incident instead.

Step six. They restore the baseline setting, and they check the server once more to confirm that it is correct.

Step seven. They speak to the technician and find out why the service was needed. If there is a real need, it must go through change management, and the baseline must be updated.

Step eight. They look for the cause. Technicians had no approved way of moving large files. So the team provides a secure file transfer tool, which removes the temptation to switch on file sharing.

Notice that the automated tool found the problem, but people judged what it meant. Notice also that the final answer was not simply to reset one setting.

The exam will often give you a problem that keeps coming back. The best answer usually deals with the master image, the baseline or the process, and not with each machine separately.

Here is your takeaway. Detect the drift, check for approval, consider an attack, restore the baseline, and fix the reason it happened.

keyTerms.meaning: Keeping systems set up in a known, approved and recorded way.
Preparing and delivering a new system so it is secure from day one.
An approved record of how a system should be set up, used for comparison.
When a system slowly moves away from its approved setup.
Configuration management database: the central record of systems and their settings.
An approved master copy used to build new systems.
Writing system setup in files that can be reviewed, reused and version-controlled.

keyPoints: A baseline is the approved setup you compare against.
Provision new systems from a hardened image.
Automation gives consistency but can spread mistakes quickly.
Update the baseline whenever an approved change affects it.
topics.memoryHook: Baseline is the recipe. Provisioning is cooking from the recipe. Drift is when the cook starts adding extra salt.

question.prompt: An audit finds that many servers no longer match the approved standard because administrators have made small manual fixes over time. Which action would BEST solve this problem over the long term?
options: Hold an audit of every server once a year
Remind administrators at every staff meeting to follow the approved standard
Make administrators use longer and stronger passwords
Automatically compare servers to the baseline and correct drift
question.explanation: Automated comparison finds drift as it happens and can correct it. A yearly audit is tempting, but it finds problems up to a year late and fixes nothing by itself.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company needs to find every server running one particular software version, within an hour of a new attack being announced. Which resource would help MOST?
options: An up-to-date configuration management database
The minutes from the change advisory board's last meeting
The firewall rule list
The disaster recovery plan
practiceQuestions.explanation: A configuration management database records what exists and how each item is set up. The change board's notes are tempting, but they record decisions about changes, not the current state of all systems.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A new server will be placed on the company network next week. To reduce risk, when should default accounts be removed and current patches applied?
options: After the first vulnerability scan of the live production network
During the first scheduled maintenance after go-live
Before the server is connected to the production network
As soon as users report that they can log in
practiceQuestions.explanation: Provisioning should make a system secure from its first day, so hardening happens before it goes live. Waiting for the first maintenance window is tempting for convenience, but the server is exposed throughout that time.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A published security benchmark includes a setting that would stop an essential application from working. What should the security manager do?
options: Delete the whole benchmark and write a new one from scratch
Apply the setting anyway because the benchmark is authoritative
Ask administrators to leave that one setting as they see fit
Record an approved exception and add a compensating control
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tailoring allows a documented exception with a compensating control. Applying the setting anyway is tempting because it follows the guide, but it would break an essential business function.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An organisation writes its server setups in files that are version-controlled and reviewed before use. What is this practice called?
options: Golden imaging
Infrastructure as code
Configuration status accounting
Vulnerability management
practiceQuestions.explanation: Writing system setup in reviewable files is infrastructure as code. Golden imaging is tempting because it also builds systems consistently, but it uses a master copy of a system and not setup files.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A faulty setting in an automated build tool reached every branch office server within ten minutes. Which control would BEST reduce this risk in future?
options: Stop using automation and build each server manually
Run the tool only at night when nobody is working
Review changes and release them to a small test group first
Give more staff permission to change the build files
practiceQuestions.explanation: Review and staged release catch a bad setting before it spreads. Dropping automation is tempting after a failure, but it gives up consistency and brings back human error.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An auditor wants to confirm that what is running in production really matches the approved records. Which activity does this describe?
options: Provisioning
Configuration auditing
Tailoring
Regression testing after an upgrade
practiceQuestions.explanation: Configuration auditing compares reality with the records. Regression testing is tempting because it is also a check, but it tests whether software still works after a change.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An approved change alters a security setting on all database servers. The change has been completed. What else should be updated to prevent the old setting from coming back on new builds?
options: The security awareness training slides
The company's business impact analysis
The service level agreement
The configuration baseline and the master image
practiceQuestions.explanation: The baseline and master image must match the approved state, so new systems start correctly. The business impact analysis is tempting because it is a key document, but it records business priorities and not settings.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A network tool discovers a device that is not listed in the configuration management database. What should the security team do FIRST?
options: Investigate what the device is and who connected it
Add it to the database so that the records agree
Shut down the whole network segment immediately as a precaution
Ignore it unless it starts causing problems
practiceQuestions.explanation: An unknown device could be harmless or could be a rogue device, so the team must find out. Adding it to the database is tempting for tidy records, but that would approve something nobody has checked.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A department creates cloud servers using its own credit card. The servers appear in no record and nobody patches them. What is the BEST long-term response?
options: Scan the public internet once a year for the company's servers
Ban every use of cloud services across the whole company
Bring cloud provisioning under the approved, recorded process
Ask the department to keep its own spreadsheet of the servers
practiceQuestions.explanation: An approved process means new servers are hardened, recorded and patched. A ban is tempting, but it ignores the business need and tends to push the activity further out of sight.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between change management and configuration management?
options: Change management records system settings, while configuration management approves changes
Configuration management applies only to hardware, and change management to software
They are two names for the same process
Change management decides on a change, and configuration management records the resulting state
practiceQuestions.explanation: One gives permission for a change, and the other records and checks how things stand. The first option is tempting because it uses the right words, but it swaps the two roles.

topics.name: Foundational security operations
topics.simpleExplanation: These are the everyday rules for who may do what. Need to know means you see only the information your job requires. Least privilege means you get only the rights your job requires. Separation of duties means one person cannot finish a risky task alone. Job rotation moves people between roles so that hidden problems come to light. Powerful accounts get extra watching. A service level agreement writes down what a supplier promises. Think of a bank, where no one person holds all the keys.

studyNotes.heading: Need to know and least privilege
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at need to know and least privilege. These two ideas are close, but they are not the same.

Need to know is about information. You may see something only if your work requires it. Think of a family doctor's office. The receptionist may need your appointment time, but does not need to read your medical history. Even someone with a high security clearance has no need to know about a secret project that lies outside their work. Clearance tells you what level a person may be trusted with. Need to know tells you whether they should see this particular thing.

Least privilege is about rights and actions. You receive only the permissions your job requires, and no more. Think of a hotel cleaner's key. It opens the guest rooms on one floor during working hours, but not the safe in the manager's office.

Here is a workplace example. A help desk worker can reset a password, but cannot delete all user accounts. A payroll clerk can enter hours, and can read the records for one department, but cannot change the tax tables.

Notice how the two fit together. Need to know limits what you can see. Least privilege limits what you can do.

These ideas apply to systems as well as people. A program that only needs to read a database should not run with an account that is able to delete it. If an attacker takes over that program, the harm is limited.

Privilege creep happens when someone changes jobs over time and keeps their old rights as well as the new ones. After ten years, a long-serving employee may have more access than anyone realises. Regular access reviews catch this problem. A manager looks at who has what, and confirms whether it is still needed.

A related idea is default deny. Start with no access at all, and add only what is justified. That is safer than starting with everything, and trying to remove what is not wanted.

Here is what to take away. Need to know is about information, least privilege is about rights, and regular access reviews stop privilege creep.

studyNotes.heading: Separation of duties and responsibilities
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at separation of duties, which stops any one person from having too much power.

Separation of duties, often called SoD, splits a sensitive task so that no single person can complete it alone. Think of a shop. One person orders the goods, another checks that they arrived, and a third pays the bill. If one person could do all three, that person could invent a supplier and pay themselves.

Here is a workplace example from technology. A developer writes the code, a separate person tests it, and an operations team moves it into production. Production means the live systems that the business really uses. The developer cannot sneak in a change, because someone else has to release it.

A similar example involves security logs. The administrator who runs a system should not be the only person who can read or delete the logs of that system. Otherwise, that administrator could hide any misuse.

Collusion means two or more people secretly working together to break the rules. Separation of duties makes fraud harder, because fraud now needs collusion. It does not make collusion impossible. It simply raises the difficulty and the risk of being discovered.

There are some related controls that the exam expects you to recognise.

Two-person control means that two people must act together at the same time, such as two keys being turned for a vault. Think of the old films where two officers turn their keys at the same moment.

M of N control means that a set number of people out of a larger group must agree. For example, any 3 of 5 managers must provide their part of a key before a master encryption key can be recovered.

Split knowledge means that no single person knows the whole secret. Each person holds only one part.

Sometimes a very small team cannot separate duties. A company with two technology staff cannot have three separate roles. In that case, use a compensating control, such as an independent review of the logs by someone outside the team. A compensating control is another protection used when the normal one is not possible.

Here is your takeaway. No single person should complete a sensitive task alone, and when that cannot be done, add a compensating control.

studyNotes.heading: Job rotation and mandatory vacations
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at job rotation and mandatory vacations. They are both simple ideas, and they can be surprisingly powerful.

Job rotation moves staff between roles from time to time. Think of a team of shop assistants who take turns on the till, on the shop floor and in the store room. Each person learns the whole business. If one is ill, somebody else can step in.

This practice has two main benefits.

The first is that it finds hidden fraud. A new person in the role looks at the records with fresh eyes. Things that were being hidden can suddenly come to light.

The second benefit is cross-training. Staff learn other roles, so the business does not depend on one person. Many organisations have a dangerous habit of relying on one expert, the only one who knows how an old system works. If that person leaves, wins the lottery, or falls ill, the business is in trouble.

Mandatory vacations are closely related. A person is required to take a block of leave, often at least one full week or two, and somebody else does the work in the meantime. Fraud that needs daily hiding is often found this way.

Here is a workplace example. A bank's accounts clerk is the model employee, and has not taken a day off in five years. When the bank enforces its leave policy, a colleague takes over for two weeks and notices payments going to an unknown account. The clerk had been moving small amounts for years. The fraud could continue only as long as the clerk was present to cover it each day.

That clerk's loyalty looked like a good thing. In fact, an employee who never takes leave can be a warning sign.

These are detective controls, which means they help to discover problems. Separation of duties is largely a preventive control, which means it stops problems from happening. They work best together.

For these controls to work, access must be arranged carefully. The person who steps in needs the rights to do the job, and the person who is away should not be able to log in remotely and keep covering their tracks.

Here is what to take away. Job rotation and mandatory vacations reveal hidden fraud, and rotation also reduces dependence on one person.

studyNotes.heading: Privileged account management
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at how powerful accounts are controlled.

PAM stands for privileged account management. A privileged account is one that can do far more than a normal account, such as an administrator on a server or the owner of a cloud subscription. Think of the master key for a block of flats. Nobody leaves it under the doormat, and the caretaker signs for it whenever it is used.

These accounts can do the most harm. An attacker who gets one can create new accounts, switch off logging and read everything. So they get the tightest control.

The main practices are these.

Give each person their own account. Avoid shared accounts, because then nobody can be held accountable. Accountability means being able to tie an action to one person.

Require MFA, or multi-factor authentication, which means more than one kind of proof, such as a password and a code from a phone.

Grant high rights only when needed, and only for a short time. This is called just-in-time access. For example, an engineer asks for administrator rights for two hours for one approved task, and the rights then disappear.

Store passwords in a vault. A vault is a secure system that holds passwords, hands them out only to approved people, and changes them after use.

Record and review privileged sessions, so that there is a record of what was done. The person reviewing the sessions should be someone other than the person who did the work.

Keep normal work, such as reading email, on a separate normal account. If an administrator opens a malicious attachment while logged in with full rights, the attacker gets those full rights too.

Service accounts deserve attention too. These are accounts used by programs, not by people. They are often forgotten, have passwords that never change, and hold more rights than needed.

Here is a workplace example. A company puts all of its administrator passwords into a vault. To use one, an engineer logs in with multi-factor authentication and gives a ticket number. The session is recorded, and a security analyst spot-checks a sample each week.

Here is your takeaway. Privileged accounts need individual ownership, strong authentication, short-lived rights, a vault, recorded sessions and regular review.

studyNotes.heading: Service level agreements
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at service level agreements, which turn a supplier's promises into something that can be measured.

An SLA, or service level agreement, is a contract that sets measurable promises from a provider. Think of a pizza shop that promises delivery within thirty minutes or the pizza is free. The promise is clear. You can measure it, and there is a stated result if it is broken.

A typical agreement states these things: how much uptime is promised, how quickly a problem will be answered, how quickly it will be fixed, and what penalty applies if the provider fails. Uptime means the time during which a service is working.

Two measures often appear. MTBF, or mean time between failures, is the average time that something runs before it breaks. MTTR, or mean time to repair, is the average time to fix it.

Now a worked example. An agreement promises 99.9 percent uptime each month. How much downtime is allowed?

A 30-day month has 720 hours. That is 30 times 24. The allowed downtime is the remaining 0.1 percent. So we work out 720 times 0.001, which is 0.72 hours. Now turn that into minutes. 0.72 times 60 is about 43 minutes.

So a provider who promises 99.9 percent may be down for about 43 minutes in that month, and still be keeping its promise. If you tighten it to 99.99 percent, the allowance drops by ten times, to about 4 minutes. Each extra nine costs a great deal more money, so a business should buy only what it really needs.

Be careful about the wording. Check how downtime is measured, and whether planned maintenance counts.

Here is the manager's view. You can hand over the work, but you remain accountable for the risk. If a cloud provider loses your customers' data, your customers will still blame you. So check the provider's reports. Do not simply assume that they are meeting the agreement. For security, an agreement may also include how quickly the provider must tell you about a breach.

The exam may also mention an MOU, or memorandum of understanding. That is a less formal statement of intent, and it usually carries no penalties.

Here is what to take away. An agreement must be measurable, the numbers matter, and accountability stays with you.

studyNotes.heading: Putting the foundations together
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will bring these ideas together, and see how they work in one realistic situation. We will also look at how to choose between them on the exam.

Think of a house with several safeguards. The lock stops someone getting in. The alarm tells you if they do. The neighbour who visits while you are away may notice something odd. Each one does a different job. Security operations concepts are the same. They overlap, and they support one another.

Here is a worked example. A mid-sized insurance company has just suffered a fraud. A claims supervisor approved fake claims and paid them to a friend, over three years. An investigation reveals the following. The supervisor could both create and approve a claim. The supervisor had not taken a holiday in three years. The supervisor still had rights from an earlier job in the finance team. Nobody reviewed the supervisor's activity.

Now we match each weakness to a concept.

Creating and approving a claim by the same person is a failure of separation of duties. So split those tasks between two people.

The missing holiday points to mandatory vacations. So enforce a leave policy.

The old finance rights are privilege creep, and they break the principle of least privilege. So start regular access reviews, and remove old rights whenever someone changes roles.

The lack of review points to weak monitoring. So let an independent person review the logs of high-value payments.

Now here is how to choose on the exam. Read the scenario, and ask what the actual problem is.

If somebody can see something they should not, think about need to know.

If somebody can do something they should not, think about least privilege.

If one person can complete a risky process alone, think about separation of duties.

If fraud is staying hidden because one person always does the job, think about job rotation or mandatory vacations.

If nobody can tell who did something, think about individual accounts and accountability.

If a supplier's promises cannot be measured, think about the service level agreement.

And as a manager, remember to fix the process and record the decision, and not just to punish one person.

Here is your takeaway. Name the real weakness first, and then pick the control that addresses that weakness directly.

keyTerms.meaning: Access to information only when your work requires it, even if you have clearance.
Giving only the rights a job requires and no more.
Splitting a sensitive task so no single person can complete it alone.
Two or more people secretly working together to break the rules.
Moving staff between roles to find fraud and to cross-train.
Collecting more rights over time as a person changes roles.
Privileged account management: tight control of powerful accounts.
Service level agreement: a contract with measurable promises from a provider.

keyPoints: Need to know is about information, while least privilege is about rights.
Separation of duties forces fraud to need collusion.
Shared accounts destroy accountability.
Regular access reviews stop privilege creep.
You stay accountable even when a provider does the work.
topics.memoryHook: A bank vault with two keys held by two people: no single person can open it, and every opening is written down.

question.prompt: Five system administrators all log in with one shared root password. An auditor says that nobody can tell who made a damaging change last month. What is the BEST solution?
options: Change the shared password every month
Give each administrator a personal account with recorded sessions
Stop administrators from logging in to production systems unless a manager is present
Keep the shared password in a locked office safe
question.explanation: Individual accounts with recorded sessions give accountability, which is the real problem here. Changing the password monthly is tempting, but everyone still shares it, so nobody can be traced.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A senior analyst holds a top-level clearance and asks to read files from a secret project that is unrelated to the analyst's work. What is the BEST response?
options: Refuse, because the analyst has no need to know
Allow it, because the clearance level is high enough
Allow it, but only for a limited period of time
Refuse, unless the analyst first signs a new confidentiality form
practiceQuestions.explanation: Clearance alone is not enough. The person also needs a work reason. Allowing it because of clearance is tempting, but need to know applies at every clearance level.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An employee has worked in sales, marketing and finance over eight years, and still has access to systems in all three departments. Which problem does this describe?
options: Separation of duties
Collusion
Privilege creep
Job rotation
practiceQuestions.explanation: Keeping old rights while gaining new ones is privilege creep. Job rotation is tempting because the person moved between roles, but rotation is a control and the leftover access is the problem.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In a company's payment system, one person creates a new supplier and another person must approve payments to it. Fraud is still possible if which of these occurs?
options: The two employees work in different buildings
The two employees secretly work together
The payments are recorded in a central log
One of the two employees takes annual leave
practiceQuestions.explanation: Separation of duties forces fraud to need collusion, but it cannot remove that possibility. Annual leave is tempting because of its link to fraud detection, but leave helps to reveal fraud and does not make it possible.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A master encryption key can be recovered only when any three of the seven appointed managers provide their part. What is this control?
options: Least privilege
Job rotation
Mandatory access control
M of N control
