practiceQuestions.explanation: A set number out of a larger group must act together, which is M of N control. Mandatory access control is tempting because of the word control, but it is a method of granting access based on labels.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A small company has only one database administrator and cannot afford a second. How can it BEST reduce the risk of misuse by that administrator?
options: Ask the administrator to sign a yearly statement of good conduct
Have someone independent regularly review the administrator's logged activity
Remove all of the administrator's access to the database
Rely on the fact that the administrator is a trusted employee
practiceQuestions.explanation: An independent review is a compensating control where duties cannot be separated. A signed statement is tempting because it is cheap, but it neither prevents nor detects anything.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A bank requires staff in sensitive roles to take two weeks of leave in a row each year while someone else performs their duties. What is the MAIN security purpose of this rule?
options: To improve staff health and reduce the number of sick days
To reduce the number of accounts that need passwords
To reveal fraud that needs daily concealment
To lower the cost of the payroll system
practiceQuestions.explanation: With the person away, someone else may see what was being hidden. Staff health is a real benefit and tempting to select, but it is not the main security reason.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A system administrator uses one account for email, web browsing and server administration. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Force the administrator to change the password every week
Install a second web browser for administration tasks
Monitor the administrator's email more closely each day
Use a normal account for daily work and a separate privileged account for administration
practiceQuestions.explanation: Separating daily activity from privileged use limits the harm if a malicious email is opened. Frequent password changes are tempting, but malware running under the account would still have full rights.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An engineer needs administrator rights for one approved task lasting two hours. Which approach BEST supports least privilege?
options: Grant just-in-time access that ends when the task is finished
Add the engineer permanently to the administrators group
Share the password of an existing administrator with the engineer
Leave the engineer's normal rights in place and skip the approved task
practiceQuestions.explanation: Just-in-time access grants rights only when needed and removes them afterwards. Permanent membership is tempting for convenience, but it leaves high rights in place long after the task.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hosting contract promises 99 percent uptime in a 30-day month. What is the MOST downtime allowed in that month without breaking the promise?
options: About 43 minutes
About 72 hours
About 7.2 hours
About 1 hour
practiceQuestions.explanation: A 30-day month has 720 hours, and 1 percent of 720 is 7.2 hours. About 43 minutes is tempting, but that is the figure for 99.9 percent uptime.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has moved its payroll to an outside provider under a service level agreement. A provider error then exposes staff salaries. Who remains accountable to the staff for this?
options: Only the provider, as it caused the failure
The company that chose to use the provider
The regulator that oversees data protection law
The individual employee who was on duty at the provider
practiceQuestions.explanation: The work can be outsourced, but accountability stays with the organisation. Blaming only the provider is tempting because it caused the error, but the provider's contract does not remove the company's duty to its staff.

topics.name: Resource protection
topics.simpleExplanation: Resource protection means looking after the things that hold your data. Media means anything that stores data, such as hard drives, tapes and USB sticks (small plug-in storage devices). Think of a school's paper records. You label them, you lock them up, you know who took them, and you shred them when they are no longer needed. Data also needs protection while it sits still and while it travels. Encryption, which scrambles data so only key holders can read it, does much of this work.

studyNotes.heading: Media management through its whole life
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at media management, which means controlling storage items from the day they arrive until the day they are destroyed.

Media is anything that stores data. Hard drives, tapes, USB sticks, which are small plug-in storage devices, and even paper all count. Think of a school's paper records. You label them, lock them up, know who borrowed them, and shred them when they are no longer needed.

The life of a piece of media has several stages.

Marking and labelling. Show the sensitivity on the item, so that people know how to handle it. A tape with no label is a danger, because someone may treat it as though it holds nothing important.

Handling. Only approved people move it, and each move is recorded.

Storage. Keep it locked, cool and dry. Keep backup media away from the main site, so that a single fire cannot destroy both copies.

Retention. Keep it only as long as policy and law require. Retention simply means holding on to something. A legal hold means that you must keep it because of a court case, even past the usual date.

Disposal. Sanitise or destroy it when it is finished with. Sanitise means removing the data so it cannot be recovered.

Media wears out. Tapes and disks have a limited life. Follow the maker's advice on how many times something can be used and how long it can be kept. Then test that you can still read it. A backup that you cannot read is not a backup at all.

Old media raises another problem. If you keep a tape for ten years, you must also keep a machine that can read it.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital sends its backup tapes to an offsite store. Each tape has a barcode and a classification label. Every hand-over is scanned, and the two sides reconcile their lists each month. When a tape reaches its retention date, the hospital checks for legal holds before ordering its destruction.

The manager's view is that the owner of the data decides how it should be classified, and the operations staff carry out the handling that this classification requires.

Here is what to take away. Label, handle, store, retain and dispose of media under control, and test that it can still be read.

studyNotes.heading: Sanitising media: clear, purge and destroy
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how to remove data properly, because deleting a file does much less than most people think.

Data remanence is data that stays behind after you try to delete it. Think of a book in a library. Deleting a file is like tearing the entry out of the catalogue. The book itself is still sitting on the shelf. Formatting a disk is much the same. The data can usually be recovered.

There are three levels. They run from weakest to strongest, and the exam expects you to know the order. They come from guidance by NIST, the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology.

- Clear: overwrite the data, so that ordinary software tools cannot recover it.
- Purge: a stronger method, so that even a laboratory cannot recover it. Examples are degaussing and cryptographic erase.
- Destroy: physically ruin the media by shredding, crushing, melting or burning.

The method must fit the type of media.

Degaussing uses a strong magnetic field to wipe magnetic media, such as tapes and older hard disks. It does not work on SSDs, or solid-state drives, which store data in chips and not on magnetic platters. It also does not work on optical discs, such as DVDs.

Overwriting is not reliable on SSDs either. These drives spread writing around their chips to make them last, which is called wear levelling. Because of this, some old data may be left in places that an overwrite never reaches.

Cryptographic erase means destroying the encryption key, so that the data can never be read. Encryption is the scrambling of data, so that only someone with the key can read it. This works very well on SSDs, provided that the data was encrypted from the start.

For the most sensitive data that will never be reused, physical destruction is the safest choice.

Here is a workplace example. A company reuses its old magnetic disks within the same department. Clearing is enough for that. However, if those disks are leaving the company, a stronger method is needed, because the risk is higher once they are out of your control.

Here is your takeaway. Clear, purge and destroy run from weakest to strongest, the method must suit the media, and degaussing does not work on solid-state drives.

studyNotes.heading: Media protection techniques
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at the techniques that protect media from theft, loss and tampering.

Think about carrying a large sum of cash. You would not leave it in a clear plastic bag on a bus seat. You would seal it, keep it with you, and use a trusted courier if you could not carry it yourself. Media deserves the same care.

These are the main techniques.

Encrypt portable media, so that a lost item does not expose data. Encryption is the scrambling of data so that only a key holder can read it. This is the single most useful protection for anything that leaves the building.

Control USB ports, using technical rules as well as policy. USB stands for Universal Serial Bus, and it is the common plug used for removable drives. Many organisations allow only approved, encrypted drives, or they block these ports altogether.

Use write protection where media should not change. A forensic copy, or a master software image, is a good example.

Use tamper-evident bags and sealed containers for moving media. These show clearly if somebody has opened them.

Use trusted couriers, and keep a record of each hand-over. Check that the number of items sent matches the number received.

Keep backup copies away from the original, but protect them just as well. A backup tape holds the same secrets as the live system. It deserves the same protection.

Control the environment. Heat, damp and magnetic fields can damage media. Store them in the conditions that the maker recommends.

Here is a workplace example. A law firm has a contract to send a case file to another office. The file goes on an encrypted drive, sealed in a tamper-evident bag. A named courier carries it, and signs a transfer record at each end. The password travels separately, by a different channel. If the bag is lost, the finder has a useless device.

The password is sent separately for a good reason. If the key travels with the lock, the lock provides no protection.

The manager would also ask whether the data needs to travel at all. Removing sensitive data that is no longer needed reduces the risk, because data you do not hold cannot be stolen.

Here is what to take away. Encrypt anything that travels, control ports, seal and track each move, and protect backups as you would protect the live data.

studyNotes.heading: Data at rest
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at data at rest, which is one of two states that the outline names for this objective.

Data at rest is data sitting in storage, such as a laptop disk, a database or a backup tape. Think of money in a safe. It is not going anywhere, but a thief could still try to break in and take it.

The main protections are encryption, access controls and backups.

Encryption is the scrambling of data so that only a key holder can read it. AES, or Advanced Encryption Standard, is the common choice of cipher. A cipher is a method of encryption. It works at different levels.

Full-disk encryption protects an entire drive. It mainly protects a stolen laptop while that laptop is switched off. Once the laptop is on and the user is logged in, the data is readable to anyone with control of that session.

File-level encryption protects individual files, so that they remain protected even when copied elsewhere.

Database encryption protects stored records. Some databases can encrypt selected columns, such as card numbers.

Access controls decide who can reach the data. Encryption does not help if everyone has the key. Backups protect availability. If the data is destroyed, you can still get it back.

Protecting the key matters as much as the encryption. If the key sits beside the data, the lock is useless. An HSM, or hardware security module, is a tamper-resistant device that creates and stores keys. Organisations use key management procedures to rotate keys and to retire them safely.

There is another option that is sometimes better than encryption. Tokenisation replaces a sensitive value with a meaningless token, with the real value held in a separate secure place. Masking hides part of the value, such as showing only the last four digits of a card number.

Here is a workplace example. A retailer encrypts its customer database, and stores the keys in a hardware security module. A thief who copies the database files gets nothing useful. But if an attacker steals a database administrator's working login, the database may serve up readable records, because that account is allowed to read them. That is why encryption is only one layer.

Here is your takeaway. Encrypt stored data, protect the keys separately, control who can reach it, and remember what each type of encryption does not protect.

studyNotes.heading: Data in transit
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at data in transit, which is the second of the two states.

Data in transit is data moving across a network, such as a payment travelling to a bank. Think of a postcard. Anyone who handles it along the way can read it. A sealed letter is better, and a locked courier box is better still. Unprotected network traffic is like the postcard.

Here are the main protections.

TLS, or Transport Layer Security, secures web traffic and many other connections. When you see the padlock in a web browser, TLS is at work. Its older relative, called SSL, or Secure Sockets Layer, should no longer be used.

IPsec, or Internet Protocol Security, protects traffic at the network level. It is often used for a VPN, or virtual private network, which is a private tunnel across the internet.

SSH, or Secure Shell, gives an encrypted connection for administering a server, and it replaces older tools that sent passwords in the clear.

There are two ways of encrypting a path. Link encryption protects each section between two devices, and the data is decrypted and encrypted again at each stop. End-to-end encryption keeps the data encrypted the whole way from sender to receiver, so that points in between cannot read it.

As with data at rest, the strength depends on doing things properly. Weak, outdated settings can be attacked. Certificates, which are the digital identity documents that prove who a server is, must be checked and kept up to date.

There is also a third state that you should recognise, called data in use. This is data being processed in memory. It is the hardest to protect, because data normally has to be decrypted to be used.

Here is a workplace example. A company's staff connect from home. Their laptops connect to the office through a VPN, and internal websites use TLS as well. A member of staff at a coffee shop is using public Wi-Fi, a wireless network that strangers can also join. Anyone listening on that network sees only scrambled traffic.

A manager would also consider whether the sensitive data should leave the network at all, and whether a data loss prevention tool should watch it.

Here is what to take away. Use TLS, IPsec or SSH for data on the move, and retire old protocols that send data in the clear.

studyNotes.heading: Worked example: retiring a batch of laptops
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will work through one complete example, from the decision to retire equipment all the way to the final record.

Think about moving out of a home that you have rented. Before you hand back the keys, you check the cupboards, take your papers, and make sure that nothing private has been left behind. You also keep a note of what you did, in case anyone asks later.

A company is replacing 200 laptops. Here are the steps it follows.

Step one. Check the data classification and any legal hold. Some of these laptops belonged to staff who are involved in a court case. Those laptops must be kept, and they are set aside.

Step two. Choose the method. These laptops use SSDs, which are solid-state drives, so degaussing will not work. Degaussing relies on magnetism, and these drives store data in chips.

Step three. Consider the destination. Some laptops will be reused within the company. Others will be sold to a recycling firm. The data held on the finance team's machines is highly sensitive.

Step four. For laptops being reused, use cryptographic erase, because the disks were encrypted from the start. Then check the result. A sample is tested to confirm that the data cannot be read.

Step five. For the laptops leaving the company with no further use, including the finance machines, the drives are removed and shredded. An approved firm does the shredding and supplies a certificate of destruction. Staff from the company watch it happen or the firm provides proof.

Step six. Record the serial number of each device, the method used, the date, and the name of the person who did it. This is the evidence that the company did what its policy requires.

Notice three points. The legal hold came first, ahead of any plan to wipe. The method matched the media. And the record was kept.

There is one more thing to remember. Printers, photocopiers and even some network devices also hold data in internal storage. These are easily forgotten when they go back to a leasing company.

On the exam, watch for details such as the type of drive, whether the media will be reused, and whether a court case exists.

Here is your takeaway. Check for legal holds, match the method to the media and its destination, verify the result, and keep the record.

keyTerms.meaning: Anything that stores data, such as disks, tapes and USB sticks.
Data that remains after an attempt to delete it.
Overwriting data so ordinary software tools cannot recover it.
Removing data so even a laboratory cannot recover it.
Wiping magnetic media with a strong magnetic field. It does not work on SSDs.
Destroying the encryption key so that the data can never be read.
Data sitting in storage.
Data moving across a network.
An order to keep data because of a court case, even past its normal date.

keyPoints: Deleting and formatting do not remove data safely.
Clear, purge and destroy go from weakest to strongest.
Degaussing does not work on SSDs.
Backups need the same protection as the live data.
Encrypt data at rest and in transit, and protect the keys.
topics.memoryHook: Clear, Purge, Destroy: wipe the board, scrub the board, burn the board.

question.prompt: A company is getting rid of solid-state drives that hold its most sensitive data. The drives will never be reused. Which method is BEST?
options: Degauss each drive with a strong magnet
Format each drive and overwrite it once
Physically shred each drive
Delete the files and empty the recycle bin
question.explanation: Physical destruction is the surest method when the drives will not be reused. Degaussing is tempting, but it does not work on solid-state drives because they do not store data magnetically.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company stores old backup tapes, and a lawsuit has just been filed that relates to the data on them. The tapes have reached their normal destruction date. What should the company do?
options: Destroy them, because the retention period has ended
Keep them, because a legal hold overrides the normal schedule
Overwrite them, and keep a written record of the action
Send them to the other party in the lawsuit
practiceQuestions.explanation: A legal hold requires the data to be kept even past its normal date. Destroying them is tempting because policy says the time is up, but doing so could be treated as destroying evidence.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An employee deletes a confidential file and empties the recycle bin. Why might the data still be recoverable?
options: Because of data remanence
Because of data classification
Because of the data owner
Because of the retention policy
practiceQuestions.explanation: Data that remains after an attempt to delete it is called data remanence. A retention policy is tempting because it concerns how long data is kept, but it has no effect on how deletion works.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants to sanitise magnetic tapes so that even a laboratory could not recover the data, and the tapes do not need to be reused. Which method fits BEST?
options: Formatting the tapes
Deleting the files with the operating system
Clearing them with a single software overwrite
Degaussing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Degaussing is a purge method that works on magnetic media. A software overwrite is tempting, but clearing only defeats ordinary software tools.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has encrypted all its solid-state drives from the first day of use. The drives will be reused within the company. Which sanitisation method is the BEST fit?
options: Degaussing the drives
Formatting the drives
Cryptographic erase
Shredding the drives
practiceQuestions.explanation: Destroying the key makes the data unreadable and leaves the drive usable. Shredding is tempting because it is the strongest method, but the drives are meant to be reused.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Staff keep plugging unknown USB sticks into office computers, and one of them carried malware. Which control would BEST reduce this risk?
options: Send a monthly email asking staff to take care with USB sticks
Increase the required length of staff account passwords
Move the office computers to a different floor of the building
Technically block USB ports except for approved, encrypted drives
practiceQuestions.explanation: A technical control on the ports works every time, whatever staff remember. A monthly email is tempting, but a reminder alone does not stop someone from plugging in a stick.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A laptop with full-disk encryption is stolen from a meeting room. It was logged in and unlocked at the time. What is the MOST accurate statement about the data?
options: The data is safe, because the disk was encrypted
The data is safe, unless the thief can guess the password
The data may be readable, because the system was running and unlocked
The data has already been erased by the encryption software
practiceQuestions.explanation: Full-disk encryption mainly protects a device that is switched off. Saying the data is safe is tempting, but an unlocked session has already made the data readable.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A database holds card numbers. The company wants staff in customer service to see only the last four digits. Which technique is BEST?
options: Masking
Hashing the entire database
Full-disk encryption
Clearing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Masking hides part of a value, so only the permitted portion is displayed. Full-disk encryption is tempting because it protects data, but it protects the stored disk and not what staff see on screen.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An employee will connect to company systems from a hotel's public wireless network. Which control BEST protects the data while it is moving?
options: A virtual private network connection
Full-disk encryption on the laptop
A cable lock for the laptop
A stronger login password for the laptop
practiceQuestions.explanation: A virtual private network protects data in transit through an encrypted tunnel. Full-disk encryption is tempting, but it protects data at rest and not data crossing the hotel network.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A web application encrypts its database and keeps the encryption key in a file on the same server. An auditor raises this as a finding. What is the MAIN problem?
options: The encryption is too strong for that database
The key is stored alongside the data it protects
The database should have been in a different country
The key should have been shorter so it can be used more quickly
practiceQuestions.explanation: An attacker who reaches the server can get both the data and the key. A shorter key is tempting for speed, but it would weaken protection and leave the real problem in place.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company returns leased photocopiers at the end of a contract. What should the security manager make sure happens FIRST?
options: The maintenance contract is renewed for another term
The toner cartridges are removed and recycled
The copiers are cleaned to remove any fingerprints
Any internal storage in the copiers is sanitised
practiceQuestions.explanation: Many copiers store images of documents on internal disks, so those must be sanitised. Removing the toner is tempting as an obvious task, but it does nothing about stored copies of documents.

topics.name: Incident management
topics.simpleExplanation: An incident is an event that harms, or threatens to harm, your systems or data. Incident management is a planned way to handle it. Think of a house fire. You notice the smoke, you call for help, you stop the fire spreading, you tell the people who need to know, you repair the damage, you fix the faulty wire that caused it, and then you talk about how to do better next time. The exam expects you to know these seven steps in order.

studyNotes.heading: Events, incidents and being prepared
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what an incident really is, and at what must be ready before one happens.

An event is anything that happens on a system, such as a login or a file being opened. An incident is an event that harms, or could harm, the confidentiality, integrity or availability of data and systems. Confidentiality means keeping secrets. Integrity means keeping things correct. Availability means keeping things working.

Think of a home. A car driving down your street is an event. A car that crashes through your fence is an incident. Most events are harmless, and part of the job is sorting them.

The process of sorting and ranking is often called triage, a word borrowed from hospitals. In an emergency room, a nurse looks at each patient quickly and decides who needs care first. Security teams do the same. They ask what is affected, how serious it is, and how fast it is spreading.

Incident management needs preparation. A written plan, approved by senior management, sets out who does what. A trained group of people carries it out. This group is often called a CSIRT, or computer security incident response team. A good team includes technical staff, and also people from legal, human resources, communications and the business.

A plan should clearly define what counts as an incident, who has the authority to act, and how to contact each person. An incident is a very bad time to discover that nobody has the right phone number.

The team also needs tools, such as forensic software, clean spare equipment, and a way to communicate that does not depend on the systems that are under attack.

Here is a workplace example. A staff member reports that their computer is behaving strangely. The help desk records that event and checks it. If it turns out to be a slow update, it stays an event. If it turns out to be malware, which is harmful software, it becomes an incident, and the plan begins.

The exam expects you to know seven steps, and they come next. Preparation is not one of the seven, but none of the seven will work without it.

Here is what to take away. An incident harms or threatens confidentiality, integrity or availability, and the plan and team must exist before the trouble does.

studyNotes.heading: The seven steps: detection and response
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the seven steps of incident management in the order that ISC2, the body that runs this exam, lists them. Learn this exact order.

- Detection.
- Response.
- Mitigation.
- Reporting.
- Recovery.
- Remediation.
- Lessons learned.

Think of a house fire. You notice the smoke. You call for help. You stop the fire spreading. You tell the people who need to know. You repair the damage. You fix the faulty wire that caused it. Then you talk about how to do better next time. That is the whole list, in order, in one picture.

Let us take the first two now.

Detection is when something shows that all is not well. It might be a monitoring alarm, a log entry, or a worried member of staff. Someone must then confirm that it is real and not a false alarm. Tools that help include an IDS, or intrusion detection system, and a SIEM, which stands for security information and event management, a system that gathers logs in one place.

Detection often comes from people. So staff should be told exactly how to report something odd, and they should never be blamed for reporting a false alarm.

Response is when the team is activated. A person with authority declares that this is an incident and starts the plan. The team begins working and keeping records of what was seen, when, and what was done. From this point on, evidence must be protected, because the incident could end up in court.

The team also judges the severity and decides who else must join. Speed matters, and so does staying calm and following the plan.

Here is a workplace example. At nine in the morning, a monitoring tool warns that a server in the finance department is sending large amounts of data to an unknown address. An analyst checks and confirms that this is not a normal transfer. That is detection. The analyst calls the incident manager, who starts the plan and calls the team together. A shared written log is opened, with the time of each action. That is response.

Notice that nobody has unplugged anything yet. Careless action in the first few minutes can destroy evidence.

Here is your takeaway. Detection confirms that something is really wrong, response activates the team, and records begin straight away.

studyNotes.heading: Mitigation and reporting
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at the third and fourth steps, which are mitigation and reporting.

Mitigation means limiting the damage. In this step, the aim is containment, which means stopping the problem from spreading. Think of a leaking pipe in a kitchen. The first thing to do is to turn off the water. Replacing the pipe comes later.

Containment might involve taking an infected computer off the network, disabling a compromised account, or blocking an address at the firewall. A firewall is a device that controls what network traffic may pass.

The key lesson is that you contain before you try to repair.

How you contain also matters. Disconnecting a machine from the network stops the spread, and it keeps the memory intact, because the machine stays on. Powering it off destroys the contents of memory, and this may be valuable evidence. So isolate first, unless people's safety requires something else or the plan says otherwise.

Reporting is the next step. Tell management and the right people. Laws or contracts may require you to tell regulators or customers within a set time. For example, the General Data Protection Regulation, the European Union's privacy law, generally requires notice to the supervising authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach.

Reporting has its own place in the list, but in practice it continues throughout the incident. Management needs updates as the situation changes. Reports should stick to facts. Legal staff should review anything that leaves the organisation, and only named people should speak to the press or to customers.

Here is a workplace example. Let us return to the finance server that was sending out data. The team disconnects the server from the network, but leaves it running. It also disables the account that was being used. That is mitigation. The incident manager then tells the chief information security officer and the legal team. Legal finds that the data includes personal records, and starts working on who must be told, and by what date. That is reporting.

The manager's mindset is important in this step. Your duty is to advise and escalate. Decisions on what to tell the public belong to senior management.

Here is what to take away. Contain before you repair, isolate and do not power off, and report to the right people within the legal time limits.

studyNotes.heading: Recovery, remediation and lessons learned
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at the last three steps, which are recovery, remediation and lessons learned.

Recovery means returning systems to normal working order. That may involve rebuilding a machine or restoring clean backups. Check that the systems are clean and working before they go live again. Be careful that the backup you are restoring was not already infected. Monitor the restored systems closely for a while.

Think of a burst pipe. Recovery is drying the floor and turning the water back on, so that the family can use the kitchen again.

Remediation means finding the root cause and removing it. Root cause means the real reason it happened. Also check other systems for the same weakness. In the case of the pipe, remediation is finding out that the pipes are old and that they are all the same type, and then replacing them.

Many people mix up recovery and remediation. Recovery brings the service back. Remediation stops it happening again. If you only recover, the attacker can return in the same way.

The root cause is often deeper than the first answer. An unpatched server might be the obvious cause. But why was it unpatched? Perhaps nobody owned it. Then the true fix includes giving the server an owner and improving the patching process.

Lessons learned is a review of what happened, held after the incident is over. Ask what worked and what did not. Ask how the event could have been detected sooner. Then update the plan, the training and the controls. The aim is improvement, and not blame. If people are afraid of blame, they will hide what really happened.

The meeting should take place soon after the event, while memories are fresh, and it should produce a written report and a list of actions, each with an owner and a date. Senior management should see the results.

Here is a workplace example. The finance server is rebuilt and restored, and tested. That is recovery. Investigators find that an old web component was never patched, so the team patches it and checks all other servers. That is remediation. Two weeks later, the team meets and agrees that the alert should have been seen earlier, so it improves the monitoring. That is lessons learned.

Here is your takeaway. Recovery restores the service, remediation removes the cause, and lessons learned improves the process.

studyNotes.heading: Worked example: ransomware at a retail chain
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to walk through one incident from beginning to end, using all seven steps in order.

Ransomware is harmful software that locks your files and demands payment to release them. Imagine that somebody has changed all the locks on your house and is demanding money for the keys.

A retail chain arrives at work on a Monday. Here is what happens.

Detection. Tills in three stores stop working, and a ransom note appears on the screens. Staff call the help desk, which confirms that this is real and not a technical fault.

Response. The incident manager starts the plan. The team assembles and a written record begins. Because the company's email may be affected, the team uses a separate messaging service.

Mitigation. The team disconnects the affected computers from the network, keeping them powered on to preserve memory. They shut off the links between stores to stop the spread, and they make sure that the backups are disconnected from the network too.

Reporting. They inform senior management and legal. Legal advises which authorities must be told, and how soon. Named staff prepare a message for customers. Management decides, with legal advice, not to pay the ransom. Paying does not guarantee recovery, and it can break the law in some places.

Recovery. They rebuild the computers and restore backups that have been checked to be clean. The most important systems come first, and then the rest. They watch closely for any sign of the attacker's return.

Remediation. They find that a phishing email was the way in. Phishing is a trick message that fools staff. They also find that one member of staff had far too many rights, and that remote access lacked multi-factor authentication, meaning more than one kind of proof. They fix the email filter, the rights and the remote access, and they check every store for the same gaps.

Lessons learned. They meet, without blame. They agree that the plan needs clearer contact details and a regular practice. They update the plan and train the staff.

Notice how the order works. Isolating the machines came before cleaning them. Restoring the service came before the final root cause fix, and the review came last of all.

Here is what to take away. Walk through detection, response, mitigation, reporting, recovery, remediation and lessons learned, always in that order.

studyNotes.heading: The manager's rules, and other versions of the steps
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at how a manager should behave during an incident, and at one common source of confusion on the exam.

Think of a captain during a storm. The captain does not grab a rope and start pulling. The captain makes sure that everyone is safe, follows the emergency drill, and gives clear orders.

Here are the rules to remember.

People's safety always comes first, ahead of data and ahead of evidence.

Follow the plan and the policy. Do not make things up in a panic.

Never hack back. Attacking the attacker may be illegal, and the machine that you attack may belong to an innocent person whose computer was taken over.

Do not power off a system without thinking, because memory holds evidence.

Use a separate way of communicating if the attacker may be reading your email. This is often called out-of-band communication.

Only named people speak to the press and to customers.

Escalate when the matter goes beyond your authority. Senior management decides on things like calling law enforcement or paying a demand.

Now for the confusion. Different sources use different steps. NIST, the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology, has published a widely quoted guide, Special Publication 800-61. In the edition that most books still describe, it has four phases: preparation, then detection and analysis, then containment, eradication and recovery, and then post-incident activity.

Eradication means removing the attacker and the attacker's tools. The ideas overlap with the seven steps, but the names and the groups do differ.

This exam's outline uses the seven steps. So if a question asks about the outline's order, use detection, response, mitigation, reporting, recovery, remediation and lessons learned. Be careful of questions that ask what comes next. Find out which step the scenario has reached, and then choose the very next one.

Here is a workplace example of that kind of thinking. A team has isolated an infected server and has told management. What comes next? Recovery. They should not jump ahead to the review meeting.

Also watch for the word first. If the answer choices include something that protects a human being, that is nearly always the best first action.

Here is your takeaway. Put people first, follow the plan, never hack back, and answer using the seven steps in their exact order.

question.prompt: A web server was attacked through an unpatched plugin. The team has contained the attack and restored the server from a clean backup, and the service is running again. What should the team do NEXT?
options: Patch the plugin and check other servers for the same weakness
Hold the lessons learned meeting with all involved
Close the incident because the service is running again
Rebuild the server a second time to be certain
question.explanation: Remediation comes after recovery and removes the root cause. The lessons learned meeting is tempting, but it is the last step and must wait until the weakness is fixed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A monitoring tool reports that an account has logged in from two countries within five minutes. An analyst confirms that the account has been taken over. Under the seven steps, what comes NEXT?
options: Recover the account from the most recent backup
Hold a lessons learned session with the team
Activate the response team and start the incident plan
Report the matter to the industry regulator without any delay
practiceQuestions.explanation: Detection has been confirmed, so response is next, which activates the team and the plan. Reporting is tempting because a takeover is serious, but it follows response and mitigation in the listed order.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Malware is spreading between workstations on one floor of an office. The incident team has been activated. What should the team do NEXT?
options: Isolate the affected workstations from the network
Rebuild all workstations from the approved image
Find out exactly which staff member opened the attachment
Update the incident response plan
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mitigation limits the damage, so the spread must be contained first. Rebuilding is tempting because it removes the malware, but it is recovery, and the infection would still be spreading while it happened.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A team has restored a compromised web server from a clean backup. The service is running again. A week later, the same attacker is back in using the same method. Which step was MOST likely skipped?
options: Detection
Reporting
Remediation
Response
practiceQuestions.explanation: Remediation removes the root cause, and skipping it lets the attacker return the same way. Reporting is tempting because it is also easy to skip, but telling people about the attack would not close the weakness.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During an active attack on a company's systems, an engineer suggests launching an attack against the source address to make it stop. What should the security manager do?
options: Approve it, but only for a short period of time
Approve it if the source address is outside the country
Ask the legal team to approve it after the attack is over
Refuse, because attacking back may be illegal and may hit innocent systems
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hacking back is not an option, because it may break the law, and the source is often someone else's compromised machine. A short approval is tempting as a compromise, but even a brief counter-attack carries the same legal and ethical problems.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's mail server may be compromised. The incident response team needs to discuss its plans without the attacker seeing them. What is the BEST approach?
options: Use encrypted messages sent from the company's mail server
Use an out-of-band communication channel
Hold discussions only in the company's main chat channel
Delay all discussion until the mail server has been rebuilt
practiceQuestions.explanation: An out-of-band channel does not depend on the possibly compromised systems. Encrypting messages is tempting, but an attacker controlling the mail server could still see who is talking and may reach the mailboxes.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attack is still spreading when a director demands that the incident team stop and write a full report before doing anything else. What should the incident manager do?
options: Stop all containment work and write the full report as requested
Ignore the director completely until the incident has been closed
Ask the press office to write the report on the team's behalf
Give a brief update now and carry on containing the attack
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mitigation limits the damage, and reporting continues alongside it, so a short update meets both needs. Writing the full report first is tempting because a senior person asked, but the attack would keep spreading.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An organisation holds its review meeting after a major incident. Which outcome BEST shows that the meeting has served its purpose?
options: A named employee has been disciplined for causing the incident
A written list of improvements with owners and dates has been agreed
All of the attackers have been identified by name
The incident response team has been reorganised
practiceQuestions.explanation: Lessons learned aims at improvement, with clear actions and owners. Disciplining someone is tempting as a visible result, but blame discourages honest reporting in future.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of the following is an incident and not merely an event?
options: A user logs in successfully at the normal time
A scheduled backup completes without errors
A printer runs out of paper during the day
Malware encrypts files on a shared drive
practiceQuestions.explanation: An incident harms or threatens confidentiality, integrity or availability, which malware encrypting files clearly does. A printer running out of paper is tempting because it interrupts work, but it is an ordinary event with no security impact.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A breach involving personal data has been confirmed. Managers are unsure how soon the authorities must be told. Who should the incident manager involve FIRST to answer this?
options: The legal or compliance team
The network engineering team
The company's public relations agency
The vendor of the affected application
practiceQuestions.explanation: Legal or compliance staff know which notification laws apply and the time limits. Public relations is tempting because the matter may become public, but it cannot decide what the law requires.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Following a breach, a team restores a server from last week's backup. Shortly afterwards, the same malware becomes active on it. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: The backup had already been infected before it was taken
The server's hardware was too old
The monitoring tool caused the malware to return
The restore was carried out at the wrong time of day by mistake
practiceQuestions.explanation: Backups taken after the attacker got in can include the malware, so backups must be checked for cleanliness. Old hardware is tempting as an easy explanation, but it would not bring the same malware back.

topics.name: Detective and preventive measures
topics.simpleExplanation: These are the tools that stop attacks or spot them. Preventive tools try to block trouble, like a locked gate. Detective tools notice trouble, like a security camera. Firewalls control what may pass. Allow lists and deny lists say who is welcome. Sandboxes test suspicious files in a safe place. Honeypots are fake targets that trap attackers. Anti-malware and machine learning tools find bad software and strange behaviour. No single tool is enough, so we use layers, like a house with locks, alarms and a dog.

studyNotes.heading: Firewalls and the rule that ends every list
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at firewalls, which control what traffic may pass between networks.

A firewall works much like a guard at a gate. The guard has a list of who may come in, and turns away everyone else. A firewall's list is made up of rules, and they are read from the top. The last rule should be implicit deny, which means that anything not clearly allowed is blocked.

Firewalls come in several kinds, and the outline names next-generation, web application and network firewalls.

Start with the simple ones. A static packet filter checks addresses and ports only. A port is a numbered doorway to a program. It is fast but simple, and it does not understand the conversation.

Stateful inspection remembers each conversation, so it knows whether a reply belongs to a real request. Think of a receptionist who remembers that you made an appointment.

An application proxy stands between the two sides, and it understands one application in detail. Think of a translator who speaks to each side, so that the two sides never speak directly.

An NGFW, or next-generation firewall, adds awareness of applications and users, plus built-in intrusion prevention. It can allow a video call while blocking file sharing, even if both use the same port.

A WAF, or web application firewall, protects websites from attacks such as SQL injection. SQL, or Structured Query Language, is used to talk to databases, and in this attack bad commands are typed into a web form.

A network firewall protects a whole network. A host-based firewall protects one computer.

Where you place a firewall matters. A common design is a DMZ, or demilitarised zone, also called a screened subnet. This is a separate network area that holds the public-facing servers, so that the outside world never reaches the internal network directly.

Here is a workplace example. A retailer places a WAF in front of its online shop, puts the web servers in a DMZ, and uses an NGFW between that zone and its internal systems. It also reviews the rules every quarter, because old rules that nobody remembers are a common weakness.

Here is what to take away. Every firewall should end with implicit deny, and each type understands more than the type before it.

studyNotes.heading: Intrusion systems, allow lists and deny lists
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at intrusion systems as preventive and detective controls, and at how lists are used to allow or deny.

An IDS, or intrusion detection system, is a detective control. It watches and raises an alert. An IPS, or intrusion prevention system, is a preventive control. It sits in the path of the traffic and blocks.

Think of a nightclub. A camera on the wall is like an IDS. It records and alerts, but it cannot stop anybody. A door attendant is like an IPS, because that person can actually refuse entry.

If an IPS makes a mistake, it can block real work, so tune it carefully. Tuning means adjusting the rules to fit your own environment. Often, a new IPS is first set to alert only, for a few weeks, so that the team can see what it would have blocked. Only then is blocking switched on.

An allow list names what is permitted, and blocks everything else. A deny list names what is blocked, and permits everything else. Older books call these whitelists and blacklists.

Think of a party. An allow list is a guest list at the door. A deny list is a list of people who are banned, and everyone else may walk in.

The important difference is what happens to something new and unknown. With an allow list, it is blocked by default. With a deny list, it is permitted until someone adds it to the list. So an allow list is usually stronger. But it takes more work to keep up to date, and mistakes can stop people from working.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital uses an allow list on the computers that run its medical imaging machines. Those machines run only a few programs, which rarely change, so an allow list is simple to maintain and very strong. On the general office laptops, where staff need a broad range of tools, the hospital relies on anti-malware and a deny list of known bad sites.

That example shows how the manager chooses. An allow list suits a stable and sensitive system. A deny list suits a changing environment where flexibility matters.

Here is your takeaway. An IDS detects and an IPS prevents, and an allow list blocks the unknown while a deny list permits it.

studyNotes.heading: Third-party security services
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at third-party security services, which means paying another company to help with security.

Think about home security. You could sit up every night watching your own door. Or you could pay a monitoring company whose staff watch the alarms all the time, and call you only when something happens. Most businesses face the same choice.

These are the main services to recognise.

An MSSP, or managed security service provider, can watch your systems around the clock, and can run tools for you.

A CASB, or cloud access security broker, sits between your staff and cloud services, and applies your rules. For example, it can stop staff from uploading sensitive files to a personal cloud account.

Other services include outside scanning for weaknesses, penetration testing, which is an authorised attempt to break in, and SASE, or secure access service edge, which delivers network and security functions from the cloud. DDoS protection is another common service. DDoS means distributed denial of service, where large numbers of computers flood a target so that it stops working.

These services bring skill and working hours that you may not have. A small company could never afford its own team working through every night. A provider spreads that cost among many customers.

There are risks too. You are giving an outside company access to sensitive information, so that company becomes part of your own attack surface, meaning the set of ways in which you can be attacked. It may also not know your business as well as your own staff do.

So a good manager takes these steps. Check the provider's security before you sign, often using an independent audit report. Use a contract and an SLA, or service level agreement, which sets out the written promises from the provider. Agree who does what during an incident. Agree how quickly they must tell you about a problem. Then check that the provider actually meets the agreement.

Here is a workplace example. A small insurance firm hires an MSSP for night-time monitoring. When an alert appears, the provider calls a named person at the firm, who decides what to do about the business systems.

Here is what to take away. You can outsource the work, but you stay accountable, so choose carefully and verify.

studyNotes.heading: Sandboxing
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at sandboxing, which lets you find out what something does without letting it do any real harm.

A sandbox is a closed, safe space for running suspicious software. Think of a child's sandbox in a park. Whatever gets built or knocked over inside the box stays inside the box.

Security teams use a sandbox to see what a file really does. Does it try to contact a strange address? Does it try to change system files? Does it start encrypting things? Anti-malware tools looking for known patterns can miss a new file. Watching what it does in a sandbox can reveal the danger.

There are two common uses.

The first is as a security tool. Email gateways and network devices may send suspicious attachments to a sandbox automatically, before delivering them to staff. An email gateway is a system that checks mail on its way into an organisation.

The second is as part of normal application design. Web browsers and mobile phones run each program or page in its own confined space. If one part is attacked, the damage is held inside that space, away from the rest of the device.

A sandbox is often built using virtualisation. Virtualisation means running a software-based computer on top of real hardware. Because that virtual machine can be restored to a clean state within seconds, it is ideal for testing harmful files.

There is a limit to this. Clever malware can sometimes tell that it is being watched, and it behaves innocently until it reaches a real computer. It might wait an hour, or it might check for signs of a real user, such as mouse movement. So a clean result from a sandbox does not prove that a file is safe.

The sandbox must also be kept apart from the production network. Production means the systems that the business really uses. If it is connected, a harmful file could escape.

Here is a workplace example. A law firm receives an invoice attachment from an unknown sender. The email gateway opens it in a sandbox, and sees it reach out to a suspicious address and try to download more code. The message is quarantined, and it never reaches the staff member.

Here is your takeaway. A sandbox shows what a file does, safely, but a clean result is not a guarantee.

studyNotes.heading: Honeypots and honeynets
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at honeypots and honeynets, which are traps built to attract attackers.

A honeypot is a fake system built to attract attackers. A honeynet is a whole network of honeypots. Think of leaving a small jar of honey in a garden shed, well away from the picnic, so that the wasps gather there and you can watch them.

The key idea is simple. No real user has any reason to touch a honeypot. So any visit to it is suspicious. That gives a very clean signal, with few false alarms.

Honeypots have three main purposes. They help you to detect attackers who have already got inside. They help you to learn attackers' methods and tools. And they waste attackers' time, which keeps them away from the real targets.

There is also a smaller version of the same idea. A honeytoken is a piece of fake data, such as a made-up account or a false customer record. If anyone ever uses it, you know that someone has been where they should not be. A pseudo flaw is an apparent weakness placed on purpose to attract and distract an attacker.

These traps must be run carefully.

Keep them apart from real systems. If an attacker takes over the honeypot, it must not become a stepping stone to something that matters.

Hold no real data on them. Fake data is enough.

Stay on the legal side. Enticement means leaving something available for someone who is already looking to attack, and that is allowed. Entrapment means persuading someone to commit a crime that they would not otherwise have committed, and that is not allowed. So a honeypot that simply exists is fine. Advertising it on criminal forums with a promise of free data is a problem.

A manager should also get legal advice and approval before setting up a honeypot, and also check how the evidence might be used.

Here is a workplace example. A bank places a fake database on a small isolated segment of its internal network. It holds invented customer names. An alert fires when an internal account tries to read it, which reveals a stolen account that no other tool had noticed.

Here is what to take away. Any visit to a honeypot is suspicious, keep it isolated, and remember that enticement is legal and entrapment is not.

studyNotes.heading: Anti-malware, machine learning and layering
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at anti-malware tools, at machine learning and artificial intelligence based tools, and at why no single tool is enough.

Malware is harmful software. It includes viruses, worms, trojans and ransomware. Anti-malware finds it and removes it.

Signature-based tools match known malware, so they need frequent updates. Heuristic tools look at how a program behaves, so they can find new malware, but they make more mistakes. EDR, or endpoint detection and response, goes further. It records what happens on a computer and allows a team to investigate and respond. An endpoint is a device that people use, such as a laptop.

Think of a doctor. A blood test for one known disease is like a signature. Noticing that a patient looks unwell, even without knowing why, is like a heuristic.

Anti-malware works best at several layers, such as the email gateway, the web gateway and the user's computer. It also pays to use more than one vendor in different layers, so that one vendor's blind spot is less likely to matter.

Machine learning tools are trained on large amounts of data, so that they can spot unusual patterns. Artificial intelligence is the broader field of systems that perform tasks calling for judgement. These tools help with scale, because no person can read millions of events.

They do have limits. Learn these, because the exam likes them.

- They are only as good as their training data.
- They can give false alarms, or miss real attacks.
- Attackers may try to poison the data that they learn from.
- Attackers can use the same techniques to improve their own attacks.
- Their decisions may be hard to explain.

People must still review and decide. A manager should not buy such a tool because of its marketing. Test it against your own data and measure the results.

Finally, all of these measures are layered, and this is called defence in depth. Think of a house with a fence, a locked door, an alarm and a dog. If one fails, the next one is still there.

Here is a workplace example. A company blocks known bad attachments at the email gateway, uses EDR on its laptops, uses machine learning to flag strange logins, and has analysts confirm the alerts.

Here is your takeaway. Combine signatures with behaviour, keep people in the loop, and never rely on a single layer.
