question.prompt: A bank wants to confirm that its recovery site can really handle the workload. It cannot accept any risk to its live services. Which type of test is BEST?
options: Simulation test
Parallel test
Full interruption test
Tabletop exercise
question.explanation: A parallel test really runs the workload at the recovery site while the main site carries on. Full interruption is tempting because it is the most thorough, but it puts live services at risk.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An organisation wants to list the disaster recovery test types from the LEAST disruptive to the MOST disruptive. Which list is correct?
options: Read-through, simulation, tabletop, walkthrough, full interruption, parallel
Read-through, tabletop, walkthrough, simulation, parallel, full interruption
Tabletop, read-through, parallel, walkthrough, simulation, full interruption
Walkthrough, read-through, tabletop, parallel, simulation, full interruption
practiceQuestions.explanation: The order runs from reading alone, through discussion and rehearsal, to really running systems. The first option is tempting because it also starts with read-through, but simulation does not come before the discussion-based tests.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Each manager at a company is sent a copy of the recovery plan and asked to check the names, phone numbers and steps for their area. Which test is this?
options: Simulation
Parallel test
Tabletop exercise
Read-through
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each person reviewing the plan alone is a read-through. Tabletop is tempting because it is also a low-risk review, but that is a group discussion of a scenario.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Team members meet in a conference room. A facilitator describes a flood and then adds new complications as they discuss what they would do. No systems are touched. Which test is this?
options: Tabletop exercise
Parallel test
Full interruption test
Read-through
practiceQuestions.explanation: A group talking through a scenario without touching systems is a tabletop exercise. Read-through is tempting because no systems are touched there either, but that is done individually and has no scenario.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants its recovery team to travel to the alternate site and carry out its response to a realistic scenario, but no live work should be moved. Which test fits BEST?
options: Read-through
Parallel test
Simulation
Full interruption test
practiceQuestions.explanation: A simulation has staff carry out their responses without switching production. Parallel is tempting because people work at the alternate site, but it really brings up systems and runs the workload there.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a test, staff bring up systems at the recovery site and process a copy of the day's orders there, while the main site carries on as normal. Which test is this?
options: Walkthrough
Full interruption test
Tabletop exercise
Parallel test
practiceQuestions.explanation: The recovery site really runs the work while the main site continues, which is a parallel test. Full interruption is tempting because real work runs at the recovery site, but in that test the main site is shut down.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An executive proposes a full interruption test for next Friday, during the busiest week of the year, in order to get it finished. What should the security professional advise?
options: Proceed, because a full test always gives the best evidence
Run it on an even busier day to make it realistic
Delay it, start with less disruptive tests and get senior approval for a suitable time
Cancel all disaster recovery testing for the year
practiceQuestions.explanation: A full interruption can itself cause a disaster, so it needs approval and careful timing, and should follow smaller tests. Proceeding is tempting because of the strong evidence, but the business risk is far too high.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a parallel test, the recovery site takes six hours to come online. The recovery time objective is four hours. What should the team do?
options: Report the result, fix the cause and retest
Change the objective to six hours in the plan
Record the test as successful, because the site did come online
Repeat the test without telling management
practiceQuestions.explanation: A missed target should be reported, fixed and tested again. Changing the objective is tempting because the problem disappears on paper, but that figure comes from what the business needs.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a simulation, a member of the public hears staff discussing a flood and calls the police. Which step would have BEST prevented this?
options: Using stronger passwords on the test systems
Telling stakeholders about the test in advance and marking communications as a test
Holding the test on an even larger scale
Moving all of the test work to the recovery site
practiceQuestions.explanation: Warning those affected and marking messages as tests stops a test being taken for a real event. Stronger passwords are tempting as a general good practice, but they do nothing about confusion over what is happening.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A bank is planning its yearly recovery test and must follow its industry's rules. Which group MOST needs to be considered for formal notice or results?
options: The company's cafeteria supplier
The local newspaper
All former employees
The banking regulator
practiceQuestions.explanation: Some industries must tell regulators about tests or send them results. The local newspaper is tempting because of the public interest, but the press has no formal role in a compliance requirement.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A test coordinator wants to make sure that a test can be stopped safely if it starts to affect live services. What should be arranged BEFORE the test begins?
options: A clear stop procedure and a named person with authority to use it
A press release about how well the test went
A plan to continue regardless of any problem that appears
An instruction that all staff turn off their phones
practiceQuestions.explanation: A clear way to stop, with a named decision maker, protects the live business. A plan to continue regardless is tempting if completion seems to matter most, but protecting operations is far more important.

topics.name: Taking part in business continuity planning and exercises
topics.simpleExplanation: Business continuity means keeping the important work of a business going during and after a disruption. Think of a bakery whose oven breaks. It might borrow an oven, sell yesterday's stock, or change what it bakes. Disaster recovery is the smaller part that restores computer systems. A security professional helps with this planning as an adviser. You make sure that security is not forgotten when things are rushed. The business owners and senior managers decide what matters most, and they accept the plan.

studyNotes.heading: Business continuity and disaster recovery are different
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what business continuity is, and at how it differs from disaster recovery.

BCP, or business continuity planning, keeps the whole business working through a disruption. It looks at people, buildings, suppliers and processes as well as technology. DRP, or disaster recovery planning, restores computer systems after a disaster. It is narrower, and it is usually a part of the wider continuity effort.

Think of a bakery whose oven breaks. Continuity is everything the owner does to keep selling bread. She might borrow an oven, sell yesterday's stock, change what she bakes or tell her regular customers what is going on. Disaster recovery is the part about getting the oven itself fixed. Think of BCP as keeping the shop open, and DRP as getting the tills and computers working again.

Both follow the same priorities: people first, then the most important business functions.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital loses its electronic patient records. The business continuity plan says that wards should switch to paper forms, so that care can continue. The disaster recovery plan says how technicians will restore the database, and in what order. Patients keep receiving care while the technical work goes on.

The objective for this topic is called participate. That word is important. As a security professional, you are one of the participants in this work, and your part is to advise. You are not the owner of the plan. The business owners and senior managers decide what matters most, and they accept the plan.

The security professional makes sure that security is not forgotten when things are rushed. During a crisis, people are tempted to prop open doors, share passwords or send data over unsafe channels. Good planning decides in advance how security will be kept up under pressure.

There are well-known standards that guide this work. ISO 22301 is the international standard for business continuity management. NIST Special Publication 800-34 is a United States guide to planning for contingencies in information systems.

Here is what to take away. Continuity keeps the business going, recovery restores the systems, and security advises while the business decides.

studyNotes.heading: The planning process and the security professional's part
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how a continuity plan is put together, and where the security professional fits in.

Think of planning a large family wedding. Someone must take charge. You must decide what really matters, and what could be dropped if the weather turns bad. You then make backup arrangements, get everyone to agree, and tell people what to do.

Here are the usual stages, in order.

- Project scope and planning: name the team and get senior management support.
- Business impact analysis: work out which functions matter most and what an outage would cost.
- Continuity planning: choose strategies and build the plans.
- Approval and implementation: senior management signs off, and the plans go live.

Senior management support comes first. Without it, there is no budget and no authority. Business leaders should be on the team, because they understand their own work best. A team made up only of technical staff will know how the servers work, but may not know which of them really matter.

Staff from legal, human resources, facilities and communications should also be involved.

The security professional's part includes these things.

Advising on risk, and helping with the impact analysis.

Making sure that controls still work at a recovery site. A recovery site with weaker security is an attractive target.

Keeping data protected when normal rules are under strain, such as when staff suddenly have to work from home.

Making sure that encryption keys and the people who can use them are available during a recovery. Encryption is the scrambling of data so that only key holders can read it. If the key is lost in the fire, the backups are useless.

Helping to plan and run exercises.

The key point is that you are an adviser. If a manager asks you to choose how much downtime the business can stand, your correct response is to bring the information and let the business owner decide.

Here is a workplace example. A retailer forms a planning team led by the chief operating officer. The security manager points out that the fallback process for taking card payments by phone would break the rules for handling card data. So the team designs a safer version.

Here is your takeaway. Senior management support comes first, business leaders take part, and security advises and protects.

studyNotes.heading: The key numbers from a business impact analysis
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at the business impact analysis and the numbers that come out of it.

A BIA, or business impact analysis, works out which functions matter most, and what would happen if they stopped. Think of your own household. If the fridge fails, you have a day or so before the food spoils. If the television fails, you can wait. If the heating fails in winter, the answer may depend on how cold it is.

Impact is measured in money, but also in other ways, such as harm to reputation, legal penalties, and risk to safety.

These are the four numbers to know.

- MTD, or maximum tolerable downtime: the longest that a function can be down before the harm is unacceptable. Some books call this the maximum allowable outage.
- RTO, or recovery time objective: the target time to bring the system back.
- WRT, or work recovery time: the time needed after the system is back, to check data and catch up.
- RPO, or recovery point objective: the most data that you can afford to lose, measured in time.

The rule to remember, said in words, is this: the recovery time objective plus the work recovery time must be no more than the maximum tolerable downtime.

Here is a way to picture them. Imagine a line in time, with the disaster in the middle. RPO looks back in time, from the disaster to your last good copy. RTO looks forward, from the disaster to the moment when the system is running. WRT follows on from that. And MTD is the cliff edge at the very end.

Who sets these numbers? The business decides how much downtime and how much data loss it can stand. The technical team then works out how to meet those figures and how much this will cost. A number should never be changed just to suit what technology can do cheaply.

Here is a workplace example. A pharmacy chain identifies its prescription system as its most critical function. Its BIA finds that after eight hours, patients could be harmed. So its MTD is eight hours, and everything else in the plan is built around that figure.

Here is what to take away. The business sets the targets, and the recovery time objective plus the work recovery time must fit within the maximum tolerable downtime.

studyNotes.heading: Worked example: checking whether a plan meets its limits
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will work through the numbers, one step at a time, and see what the adviser does with the answer.

Think of catching a train. The train leaves at nine o'clock. It takes you 30 minutes to get to the station, and 10 minutes to buy a ticket. So you have to leave home by twenty past eight, at the latest. If your taxi takes an hour, you will miss the train. The arithmetic here is exactly the same kind.

The billing system has an MTD of 24 hours. MTD means maximum tolerable downtime.

Step one. Find the longest allowed recovery time. The WRT, or work recovery time, is 6 hours. We take 24 and subtract 6, which leaves 18. So the RTO, or recovery time objective, must be 18 hours or less.

Step two. Look at the options. A cheap option recovers the system in 20 hours. Add the 6 hours of work recovery, and the total is 26 hours. That is 2 hours beyond the limit of 24. So the cheap option fails.

Step three. A more expensive option recovers in 12 hours. Add 6, and the total is 18 hours, well inside the limit. That option passes.

Step four. Now the RPO, or recovery point objective, which is the most data that you can afford to lose. Suppose that it is 4 hours. Backups or copies must then happen at least every 4 hours. A daily backup could lose up to 24 hours of data, so it would not meet this target.

Step five. Consider the cost. Suppose that the better option costs far more each year. The adviser explains the gap clearly: the cheap option will miss the limit by 2 hours, and here is what that would mean for the business.

Step six. The business owner and senior management then decide whether to pay more or to accept the risk. If they accept the risk, that decision should be written down.

Now, what must never happen? Nobody should quietly change the MTD to 26 hours, so that the cheap option looks acceptable. That number reflects real harm to the business, and it does not change just because of a budget.

Here is your takeaway. Add the recovery time and the work recovery time, compare with the limit, then explain any gap and let the business decide.

studyNotes.heading: Taking part in exercises
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at exercises, which are a central part of what this objective asks of you.

An exercise is a practice of the plan. It can be as simple as a tabletop discussion, where people talk through a made-up event, or as large as moving real work to another building. Think of a lifeboat drill on a ship. People learn where to go and what to do, and the crew finds out whether the lifeboat really works.

Exercises build confidence, show gaps, and teach people their roles. A plan that has never been practised usually breaks at the first real test.

As a participant, you should do the following.

Take part in your assigned role, and use the plan as written. If you know a shortcut that is not in the plan, the exercise cannot test what the plan really says.

Record what went wrong, rather than quietly working around it. A person who fixes a problem silently may look helpful, but the plan stays wrong, and the next person who follows it will fail.

Report results to management, and track the fixes.

Check security throughout. Did the alternate site have the right controls? Were the backups protected on their way? Could someone have used the confusion to gain access?

Exercises should include the wider business, and not only the technical teams. A continuity exercise might involve moving a department to another building, or running a process on paper for a morning, or testing whether a key supplier can respond as promised.

They should also test assumptions. A plan may assume that all staff can reach the recovery site, or work from home. What if the roads are closed, or there is a pandemic? What if the internet provider has also been affected?

Here is a workplace example. A city's water authority runs an exercise based on a long power failure. The customer service team works from a second building for a day. Everything seems fine until they notice that the backup phones need a licence that expired last year. One staff member writes that down and raises it, instead of borrowing someone's mobile and saying nothing. The fix is made within the week.

Here is what to take away. Play your role as written, record every problem, and report the findings so that they get fixed.

studyNotes.heading: Keeping the plan alive
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at how a continuity plan is kept up to date, and how a manager should think about it.

Think of a first aid box at home. It was perfect on the day you bought it. A few years later, the medicines have expired and the plasters have run out. Nobody noticed, because nobody opened it. A plan goes out of date in just the same way.

The plan needs regular maintenance, and it must be reviewed when the business changes. New systems, new suppliers and new staff can all make an old plan wrong. Linking the plan to the change management process helps. When an important system changes, someone asks whether the plan needs to change as well.

Keep versions controlled, so that everyone has the current copy.

The plan may contain sensitive information, such as the locations of sites, names, home phone numbers and system details. So it needs protection too, while staying available to those who need it.

Suppliers are an important part of continuity. If your business depends on a single provider, your plan depends on theirs. So check your key suppliers' continuity arrangements, and include what they promise in your contract. A service level agreement is a contract that sets measurable promises from a provider.

One person or group should own the plan's upkeep, or else everybody will assume that someone else is looking after it. Senior management should receive regular reports on the state of the plan.

Now let us think about the exam. The questions in this area often turn on a small number of ideas.

First, people's safety comes before everything.

Second, senior management support is needed before work begins.

Third, the business decides priorities, and security advises.

Fourth, the numbers from the impact analysis drive the choice of strategy.

Fifth, a plan that is not tested and maintained cannot be relied upon.

Here is a workplace example. A manufacturer connects its plan to its change process. When the company moves its email to a cloud service, the change form prompts a review. The plan is updated, the contact list is checked, and the next exercise tests the new arrangement.

Here is your takeaway. Keep the plan current, control its versions, protect its contents, check your suppliers and give it a clear owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Business continuity planning: keeping the whole business working through a disruption.
Business impact analysis: finding what matters most and what an outage would cost.
Maximum tolerable downtime: the longest a function can be down before harm is unacceptable.
Recovery time objective: the target time to bring a system back.
Work recovery time: the time to check data and catch up once a system is back.
Recovery point objective: the most data you can afford to lose, measured in time.

keyPoints: BCP covers the whole business, while DRP restores computer systems.
Senior management support comes first.
RTO plus WRT must be no more than MTD.
Security advises, and the business owners decide.
Plans must be exercised and kept current.
topics.memoryHook: RPO looks back at the data you lost. RTO looks forward to when you are running again. MTD is the cliff edge.

question.prompt: During a business impact analysis, the order system is given a maximum tolerable downtime of 12 hours. The technical team proposes a cheaper recovery option with a recovery time of 16 hours. What should the security professional do?
options: Approve the option because it saves money for the business
Quietly raise the maximum tolerable downtime to 16 hours to match the proposal
Choose the most expensive recovery option available
Explain the gap and let the business owner and management decide
question.explanation: The option cannot meet the limit, so the adviser explains the gap and the business decides. Changing the downtime figure is tempting, but that number comes from business impact, not from what the technical team finds convenient.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is about to begin its first business continuity planning project. Which of the following should be secured FIRST?
options: A contract for a hot site
Senior management support
A complete inventory of laptops
A list of staff home addresses
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without senior management support, the project has no budget or authority. A hot site contract is tempting because it is a concrete step, but that strategy cannot be chosen before the business needs are known.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which statement BEST describes the difference between business continuity planning and disaster recovery planning?
options: Continuity planning is only for technical teams
Disaster recovery covers the whole business, while continuity covers only computers
They are two names for the same set of documents
Continuity keeps the business running, while disaster recovery restores technology
practiceQuestions.explanation: Continuity covers the whole business, and disaster recovery is the narrower technology part. The second option is tempting because it uses the right words, but it reverses the two scopes.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A business owner asks the security manager to decide how many hours the sales system may be down. What is the BEST response?
options: Pick a number that the technical team finds convenient
Set the figure as low as possible to be safe
Provide information and help, but let the business owner set the figure
Tell the owner that this figure is not needed at all
practiceQuestions.explanation: Downtime limits come from business impact, so the business owner decides and security advises. Setting the figure as low as possible is tempting for safety, but it could waste large sums on recovery that the business does not need.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A system has a maximum tolerable downtime of 10 hours and a work recovery time of 3 hours. What is the longest acceptable recovery time objective?
options: 7 hours
10 hours
13 hours
3 hours
practiceQuestions.explanation: The recovery time objective plus the work recovery time must fit within the limit, so 10 minus 3 is 7 hours. 13 hours is tempting, but that comes from adding when you should subtract.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company states that it can afford to lose no more than 2 hours of transaction data. Which figure does this describe?
options: Maximum tolerable downtime
Work recovery time
Recovery time objective
Recovery point objective
practiceQuestions.explanation: The recovery point objective is the most data that can be lost, measured in time. Recovery time objective is tempting because it also uses hours, but it measures how long the system takes to come back.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has a recovery point objective of 1 hour. Which backup approach would FAIL to meet it?
options: Continuous replication to another site
Transaction log shipping every 15 minutes
One full backup every night
Hourly snapshots copied to the recovery site
practiceQuestions.explanation: A nightly backup could lose up to 24 hours of data, which is far beyond 1 hour. Hourly snapshots are tempting to pick as too slow, but they do meet the 1 hour limit.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A proposed recovery option would bring a system back in 20 hours. Work recovery takes 8 hours. The maximum tolerable downtime is 24 hours. What should the security professional do?
options: Explain that the total of 28 hours misses the limit, and let management decide
Approve it, as 20 hours is less than 24 hours
Reduce the work recovery time on paper to 4 hours
Raise the maximum tolerable downtime to 28 hours
practiceQuestions.explanation: 20 plus 8 is 28 hours, which exceeds the limit, and management must decide what to do. Approving it is tempting, but it ignores the work recovery time.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a continuity exercise, a staff member notices a mistake in the plan and quietly works around it so the exercise can continue smoothly. Why is this a problem?
options: The exercise will finish too quickly
The plan remains wrong, and others may fail by following it
The staff member may be asked to do more work
The exercise will cost too much money
practiceQuestions.explanation: Problems must be recorded so that the plan gets fixed. Finishing too quickly is tempting as an odd side effect, but the real harm is that the error stays in the plan.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a real disruption, staff are told to work from home using personal email, because the company's system is down. What is the security professional's BEST contribution?
options: Forbid all work until the normal system has returned
Say nothing, because the emergency overrides all rules
Advise on a secure alternative that keeps the data protected
Personally approve the use of personal email for all staff
practiceQuestions.explanation: The adviser's job is to keep work going while keeping data safe. Forbidding all work is tempting from a security view, but keeping critical functions running is the point of continuity.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has moved a key system to a new cloud provider. The continuity plan has not been updated. Which process would BEST have caught this?
options: The yearly staff satisfaction survey
Linking plan reviews to change management
The external audit of last year's accounts
The company's car parking policy
practiceQuestions.explanation: Linking the plan to change management prompts a review whenever key systems change. The accounts audit is tempting because it is a formal check, but it looks at financial records and not at continuity.

topics.name: Physical security and personnel safety
topics.simpleExplanation: Physical security protects buildings, equipment and people from real-world harm. Think of a bank, with a fence outside, a guard at the door, cameras in the hall and a locked vault inside. Layers slow an intruder down and make them easier to catch. Personnel safety means looking after staff, at work and when they travel. If there is ever a choice between protecting people and protecting equipment, people win every time. On the exam, safety is always the first answer.

studyNotes.heading: Safety comes first, and how doors should fail
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the most important rule in physical security, and at how it applies to doors.

Human life is always the top priority. Security controls must never trap people. On the exam, if one answer protects people and another protects equipment or data, the answer that protects people is correct.

Think of a shop that locks its back door to stop shoplifters. If a fire starts and customers cannot get out through that door, the shop has traded lives for stock. No manager should ever make that choice.

This rule matters for door locks. Electronic locks depend on power, so you must decide what they do when power fails.

- Fail-safe: the door unlocks so that people can get out. Use this on exit routes.
- Fail-secure: the door stays locked. Use this for a cash store or an equipment room where nobody is trapped.

Here is an easy way to remember it. Fail-safe saves people. Fail-secure secures things. Note that the word safe here refers to the safety of people.

Fire exits must work from the inside, even if this lowers security. A common design is a door that always opens from the inside, using a bar that you push, and that remains locked from the outside. Everybody can escape, but nobody can walk in. An alarm can warn staff that the door has been opened.

Physical security works in layers, starting at the outer edge and moving inwards. Think of a bank, with a fence outside, a guard at the door, cameras in the hall and a locked vault inside. This is known as defence in depth. Layers slow an intruder down, and make that person easier to catch.

Good planning follows a sequence: deter, then delay, then detect, then assess, then respond. You want to put off an intruder if you can, slow them down if you cannot, notice them quickly, and work out what is happening so that the right response can be sent.

Here is a workplace example. A data centre's main exit door unlocks in a power failure. The inner cage that holds its servers stays locked, because no one would be trapped inside it.

Here is what to take away. People come first, exits fail safe, and physical security is built in layers.

studyNotes.heading: Perimeter security controls
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at perimeter security, which means the outer edge of your property.

Think of a castle. It has a moat, a high wall, a gate with a guard, and a clear stretch of open ground around it, so that nobody can sneak up. Modern sites use the same ideas in a less dramatic way.

Fences are the most obvious control, and the exam expects you to know these heights.

- 3 to 4 feet deters casual walkers.
- 6 to 7 feet is hard to climb.
- 8 feet with three strands of barbed wire deters a determined intruder.

These are the usual figures in a United States context, and one foot is about 30 centimetres.

Bollards are short, strong posts that stop vehicles. They protect entrances from cars being driven at them, whether by accident or on purpose.

Lighting deters people and helps cameras. A commonly quoted standard is that critical areas should be lit to two foot-candles at a height of eight feet. A foot-candle is a measure of brightness. Lights should not leave dark gaps, and should not point at guards and cameras so as to dazzle them.

Gates control where people and vehicles can enter. Guards can use judgement, which no machine can, and they can respond to something unexpected. Dogs are a strong deterrent, but they bring liability concerns, as they can injure someone.

CCTV, or closed-circuit television, means cameras that record and deter. They work best when someone watches them, or when recordings are kept and reviewed.

Motion sensors and intrusion alarms detect someone crossing the boundary.

CPTED, or crime prevention through environmental design, means shaping the site to discourage crime. Low plants and open views give fewer hiding places. Well-used, visible spaces feel watched, so that a would-be intruder feels exposed.

A further point is that the perimeter also includes things like delivery areas, side gates, roof access and air vents. A strong front gate does not help if the loading bay is left open every lunchtime.

Here is a workplace example. A government building places bollards at the front, keeps its shrubs low, lights all its paths, and has one guarded vehicle gate. A camera system records all approaches.

Here is your takeaway. Learn the three fence heights, use bollards for vehicles, and design the site so that intruders have nowhere to hide.

studyNotes.heading: Internal security controls
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at the controls inside the building.

Think of a hospital. Anyone may walk into the reception area. Only staff can go through to the wards. Only certain staff can get into the pharmacy. The security increases as the space becomes more sensitive.

That idea is called secure zones. The more sensitive the room, the fewer people may enter. A data centre usually sits at the very centre of these layers.

Badges and access cards identify people and open doors, and they keep logs of who entered. Biometric readers use a part of the body, such as a fingerprint, to confirm identity.

An access control vestibule, once called a mantrap, is a small space with two doors where only one can open at a time. It stops tailgating, which is following someone through a door. A closely related word is piggybacking. In that case, the person who has access knowingly lets someone else through. Think of holding the door for a friendly stranger carrying a box.

Visitors should sign in and wear a badge that clearly shows they are visitors. They should be escorted at all times in secure areas. Visitor records should be kept.

Locks and cabinets need strict key control. Know who has each key, and change the locks if a key goes missing.

Cameras inside sensitive rooms deter misuse, and they support investigations. Be aware of privacy, because cameras in some places are not appropriate or lawful.

A clean desk policy means that sensitive papers and devices are locked away at the end of the day.

The data centre itself needs extra care. Power should be conditioned and backed up, the temperature and humidity should be controlled, and the fire suppression should be suited to the equipment. Wiring closets should be locked, since they give direct access to the network.

Use several layers, so that one failure does not expose everything. This is defence in depth.

Here is a workplace example. A research firm requires a badge at the lobby, a badge and a code at the laboratory corridor, and a vestibule at the server room. A receptionist notices a visitor walking without an escort and acts on it at once.

Here is what to take away. Security tightens as you move inward, stop tailgating, and always escort visitors.

studyNotes.heading: Emergency management and duress
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at how to keep people safe in an emergency, and at what to do under duress.

Emergency management plans for fires, storms, medical events and violence. Think of a family that has agreed on a meeting place across the street in case of a fire. Everyone simply goes to the place that was agreed.

Staff should know the exits and the meeting points. Floor wardens help people to leave and count them at the meeting point. Practise with drills. Think also about people who need extra help, such as staff who use a wheelchair and cannot use the stairs. Someone must be assigned to help them.

A written plan for this is sometimes called an occupant emergency plan. It covers what the people in a building should do. Note that it is about the safety of people, whereas a disaster recovery plan is about restoring systems.

The emergency plan also needs a means of giving instructions, such as alarms, loudspeakers, or text messages to everybody at once. Staff should never go back into a building to collect their belongings or equipment.

Duress means being forced to act under threat. Staff may have a duress code, which is a word or personal code that looks normal, but silently calls for help. A panic button does the same job. Some door systems allow a person to enter a special code that opens the door as normal, while at the same time alerting the guards.

Think of a shop worker being held up. The worker opens the till, as demanded, and presses a button under the counter with a knee. The robber sees nothing unusual. Help is already on its way.

The guidance is simple. Comply with the attacker, stay calm, and raise the alarm silently if it is safe to do so. No data is worth a life. Staff are not expected to be heroes, and a good policy says so.

Here is a workplace example. A bank employee is forced by armed men to open the back door. The employee enters the duress code and opens the door as demanded. The guards call the police and do not attempt to confront the attackers.

Here is your takeaway. Plan, drill and count people in an emergency, and under duress, comply and raise the alarm silently.

studyNotes.heading: Travel
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at the risks of working while travelling, and at what the organisation should do about them.

Think about going on holiday. You would not leave your passport lying around in a café. You would keep your valuables close, and you would find out in advance which parts of the city are safe. Work travel needs the same thinking, and there are additional risks because you are carrying the organisation's information.

Here are the main practices.

Check travel advice for the destination first. Governments publish warnings about the risks in each country.

Take a clean loaner laptop or phone, with only the data needed. Then, if it is lost or seized, little is at risk. A loaner is a device that is lent for the trip.

Use a VPN, or virtual private network, which is a protected tunnel across the internet, on public Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi is a wireless network, and a public one could be run by, or watched by, anyone.

Never leave devices unattended, including in hotel rooms.

Check import and export rules for encryption and for any data carried. Encryption is the scrambling of data so that only key holders can read it. Some countries restrict encryption products. Some can require you to unlock a device at the border. So the less you carry, the better.

Check loaner devices for tampering on return, or simply wipe them. Do not plug them straight into the company network.

Be careful of conversations too. A crowded train is not the place to discuss a confidential deal, and shoulder surfing, which means someone looking over your shoulder, is easy in an airport lounge. A privacy screen helps.

People's safety still comes first. If a member of staff is threatened at a border, the right course of action is to comply and report later. Any policy that asks people to take risks with their own safety is a bad policy.

Here is a workplace example. An executive visits a high-risk country. The company issues a clean phone and laptop with only the required documents, briefs her on the risks, and wipes the devices when she returns.

Here is what to take away. Travel with as little data as possible, protect it well, check the rules, and treat returning devices with suspicion.

studyNotes.heading: Security training and awareness
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at security training and awareness, and at the three subjects that the outline names.

Training teaches people how to do something. Awareness reminds them why it matters. Think of road safety. A driving lesson teaches you how to use the brakes. A roadside poster reminds you not to drink and drive.

The outline names three specific subjects.

Insider threat. People inside can do great harm, and they already have access. Some act on purpose, for money or out of anger. Others do damage through carelessness. Staff should know how to report concerns, and managers should be aware of warning signs, such as serious unhappiness, unexplained money, or unusual interest in matters outside the person's role.

Social media. Posting about work, travel or a new badge can help attackers. A photo of your first day at work, showing your badge, can help someone make a copy. Attackers use social media to learn names, roles and relationships for social engineering, which means tricking people into giving something away. Staff need clear guidance about what may be shared.

Two-factor authentication fatigue. Two-factor authentication means two kinds of proof at login, such as a password and an approval on a phone. In this attack, the attacker already has the password. So the attacker sends approval prompts again and again, hoping that a tired or annoyed person will approve one. It is also called push bombing. Never approve a prompt that you did not start, and report it. Technical fixes help too, such as number matching, where the person must type a number shown on the login screen.

Repeat training regularly, and test how well it works. A simple measure is the percentage of staff who report a practice phishing email. Phishing is a trick message that fools people. It is better to measure behaviour than to count how many people attended a course. Make the training suit each role, and never humiliate someone who gets it wrong, as that discourages reporting.

Here is a workplace example. A staff member receives eight phone prompts at midnight. She denies them all, and she reports them. The team finds a stolen password and resets it.

Here is your takeaway. Train by role, teach insider threat, social media and prompt fatigue, and measure behaviour.

A door stays locked when power fails, protecting what is inside.
A short strong post that stops vehicles.
A small space with two doors, where only one can open at a time. Once called a mantrap.
Following someone through a secure door without using your own access.
Crime prevention through environmental design: shaping a site to discourage crime.
Being forced to act under threat.
A word or personal code that looks normal but silently calls for help.

keyPoints: Human safety always comes first.
Exit doors must fail safe so that people can escape.
Use layers from the fence to the vault.
Under duress, comply and raise the alarm silently.
Take clean devices when travelling.
topics.memoryHook: Fail-safe saves people. Fail-secure secures things.

question.prompt: A company is fitting electronic locks to the only exit door on a staffed office floor. What should the door do during a power failure?
options: Stay locked, to protect the equipment on the floor
Stay locked until a security guard arrives with a key
Unlock, so that people can leave the floor
Unlock only for staff who present a valid badge
question.explanation: An exit route must fail safe because people's lives come first. A badge check sounds like a sensible compromise, but the badge reader may have no power, and people could be trapped.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is fitting electronic locks to a store room that holds only spare equipment. Nobody works in the room. What should the lock do during a power failure?
options: Unlock, because every door must fail safe
Stay locked, because nobody would be trapped
Unlock for one hour and then lock again
Sound an alarm and then unlock
practiceQuestions.explanation: A fail-secure lock suits a room where no one can be trapped. Unlocking is tempting because of the safety rule, but this rule is about exit routes and places where people could be trapped.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants a fence around its site that will deter a determined intruder. What is the MINIMUM it should choose?
options: 3 feet high
4 feet high
6 feet high
8 feet high with three strands of barbed wire
practiceQuestions.explanation: 8 feet with three strands of barbed wire deters a determined intruder. 6 feet is tempting, as it is hard to climb, but it is not the level given for a determined intruder.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A government office is concerned that a vehicle could be driven through its glass front entrance. Which control is BEST suited to this threat?
options: Motion sensors in the lobby
A security guard at the reception desk
Bollards in front of the entrance
A higher number of indoor cameras
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bollards are short, strong posts built to stop vehicles. A guard is tempting because guards use judgement, but a guard cannot physically stop a moving vehicle.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants to stop unauthorised people from following staff through a secure door into its data centre. Which control BEST addresses this?
options: An access control vestibule
A stronger lock on the door
A sign warning about tailgating
A longer door access code
practiceQuestions.explanation: A vestibule allows only one door to open at a time, which stops people following behind. A stronger lock is tempting, but the door is opened by a legitimate user and the follower simply walks through.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A site designer suggests trimming shrubs and placing windows that overlook the car park to reduce crime. Which approach is this?
options: Defence in depth
Crime prevention through environmental design
Separation of duties
Zero trust
practiceQuestions.explanation: Shaping the site to discourage crime is crime prevention through environmental design. Defence in depth is tempting because it is also about physical protection, but it refers to using several layers.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A fire alarm sounds. One employee wants to return to the office to collect a laptop holding sensitive data. What should happen?
options: Allow it if the laptop is close to the exit
Allow it, so long as the employee is quick
Ask a security guard to collect the laptop instead
Leave the laptop and go to the meeting point
practiceQuestions.explanation: People's lives come before any equipment or data. Asking a guard is tempting because the employee stays safe, but it only sends a different person into danger.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A staff member is being forced by an intruder to open a secure door. The staff member enters a special code that opens the door as normal and quietly alerts the guards. What is this code called?
options: A duress code
A one-time password
A master key
An M of N code
practiceQuestions.explanation: A duress code looks normal but silently calls for help. A one-time password is tempting because it is also a special code, but it is used for logging in and gives no alert.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An employee is travelling to a country where devices are often searched at the border. What is the BEST way to protect company data?
options: Carry the normal work laptop and be ready to refuse any search
Take a clean loaner device that holds only the data needed
Post the laptop to the hotel in a padded envelope
Hide the normal work laptop inside checked luggage
practiceQuestions.explanation: A clean device with minimal data means little is at risk if it is searched or seized. Refusing a search is tempting as a way to protect the data, but it can put the employee in danger.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An employee receives repeated login approval prompts on their phone at night, and did not try to log in. What should the employee do?
options: Approve one so that the prompts stop
Turn off the phone and do nothing else
Deny the prompts and report them
Ignore them until the next working week
practiceQuestions.explanation: Unexpected prompts suggest that an attacker has the password, so deny them and report it. Turning off the phone is tempting because the noise stops, but the security team would remain unaware of the attack.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants to find out whether its awareness training has changed staff behaviour. Which measure is BEST?
options: The number of staff who attended the course
The length of the course in hours
The cost of the training per person
The percentage of staff who report a practice phishing email
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reporting a test phishing email shows real behaviour. Attendance is tempting because it is easy to count, but it shows only that people were present.

examQuestions.prompt: An analyst confirms that malware is active on a file server. The company may take legal action against the attacker. What should the analyst do FIRST?
options: Power off the server at once
Disconnect the server from the network and leave it running
Wipe the server straight away and restore it from the last good backup
Email all staff to warn them about the malware
examQuestions.explanation: Isolating the server contains the attack and keeps the memory as evidence. Powering off also stops the attack, but it destroys the volatile evidence that a legal case may need.

examQuestions.prompt: A company is worried that staff may be sending customer records to personal email accounts. Which control would BEST detect this?
options: A stricter firewall rule for incoming traffic
Anti-malware software on every laptop
A longer password policy for email accounts
Egress monitoring with data loss prevention tools
examQuestions.explanation: Egress monitoring looks at what leaves the network and can recognise sensitive data. An incoming firewall rule may sound strong, but this data is going out, not coming in.

examQuestions.prompt: An auditor finds that developers write code and also move it into production themselves. What is the BEST way to fix this finding?
options: Separate the roles and release code only through the change process
Ask developers to sign a code of conduct every year and report any mistakes
Review the source code after each yearly audit
Move the developers to a separate office location
examQuestions.explanation: Separating the roles and using change control stops one person from pushing unapproved code. A signed code of conduct sets expectations, but it does not prevent anything technically.

examQuestions.prompt: An online retailer states that its order system may be down for only a few minutes and that it can lose almost no transactions. Cost is not the main concern. Which strategy BEST meets these needs?
options: A cold site with daily backups sent by courier
A warm site with nightly copies of the data
Two active sites sharing the work with synchronous data replication
A reciprocal agreement with a company in the same city
examQuestions.explanation: Two active sites with synchronous replication give the shortest recovery time and the smallest data loss. A warm site is cheaper, but it takes days to start and could lose a full day of data.

examQuestions.prompt: A company has just finished writing its first disaster recovery plan. Nobody has tested it, and management will not accept any risk to operations. Which test should be done FIRST?
options: A full interruption test on a quiet weekend
A read-through of the plan by each team member
A parallel test at the recovery site
A simulation with the whole company taking part
examQuestions.explanation: A new plan should begin with the simplest, safest test, which finds basic errors at no risk. A parallel test also protects live services, but it is costly and premature for an untested plan.

examQuestions.prompt: A robber forces a night receptionist at gunpoint to open the door to a secure area. According to good duress procedures, what should the receptionist do?
options: Comply and silently raise the alarm if it is safe
Refuse to open the door and protect the assets
Try to overpower the robber when given a chance
Open the door, then leave the building without telling anyone
examQuestions.explanation: People's safety comes first, so staff comply and use the silent alarm. Refusing may feel loyal, but no asset is worth a person's life.

examQuestions.prompt: A scanner keeps finding the same missing security setting on every new server, although the team fixes each server after the scan. What is the BEST action?
options: Run the scanner more often on new servers
Fix each new server sooner after it goes live
Accept the risk because the setting is always fixed after the scan finds it
Correct the setting in the golden image used to build servers
examQuestions.explanation: Updating the master image fixes the root cause, so new servers start correct. Scanning more often is tempting, but it only finds the same problem faster.

examQuestions.prompt: A courier company has lost a box of backup tapes on the way to the offsite store. The tapes hold customer records. Which measure would have BEST reduced the impact of this loss?
options: Encrypting the tapes before they left the building
Printing the customer records on paper as well
Choosing a courier with a lower delivery price
Sending the tapes offsite once a month instead of once a week
examQuestions.explanation: Encrypted tapes are unreadable to whoever finds them, as long as the keys are kept separate. Sending tapes less often cuts the number of trips, but any lost tape would still expose the data.

examQuestions.prompt: A small company has no security staff at night, yet attacks often begin in the early hours. It needs round-the-clock monitoring quickly and has a limited budget. What is the BEST option?
options: Hire and train a full night team of its own
Ask day staff to check the alerts each morning
Contract a managed security service provider with a clear service level agreement
Turn off remote access at night until the budget grows
examQuestions.explanation: A managed provider gives full-time coverage quickly at a lower cost, and the agreement sets measurable promises. A team of its own would work, but it is slow and costly for a small company.

examQuestions.prompt: Human resources suspects an employee of fraud. The manager asks a system administrator to log on to the employee's computer and look through the files. What should the administrator do?
options: Log on and copy any interesting files to a shared folder
Refer it to trained investigators so that a verified forensic copy can be taken
Log on quietly after hours so that the employee is not warned
Ask the employee to hand over the files voluntarily
examQuestions.explanation: Browsing the live computer changes the evidence and breaks the chain of custody, so trained staff should take a verified copy. Doing it after hours seems discreet, but it still alters the original.

reviewSession.heading: Investigations: objective 7.1
reviewSession.body: Let us go back over Domain 7 together, one objective at a time, starting with investigations. The order of volatility is the most tested idea here. Registers and cache come first. Then the routing table, the address cache, running processes and memory. Then temporary files, disk, remote logs, physical layout, and finally archive tapes. People often pick the disk image first, because it feels thorough, but memory disappears when power goes. Next, chain of custody records who held the evidence, when, where and why, with no gaps. Remember that it proves control, not truth. Criminal cases need proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and civil cases need only a preponderance of the evidence. When you choose an answer, protect the original, work on a verified copy, and call in legal early if a court is possible. Do not let a curious manager browse a suspect's computer.

reviewSession.heading: Logging and monitoring: objective 7.2
reviewSession.body: Now for logging and monitoring. Keep this simple picture in mind. An intrusion detection system alerts. An intrusion prevention system sits in the path and blocks. A security information and event management system collects logs, links them and alerts people. A security orchestration tool follows playbooks and acts. Signature detection misses new attacks, and anomaly detection catches them but makes more false alarms. The false negative is the dangerous result, because nobody knows anything happened. When a question describes staff drowning in alarms, the best answer is to tune the rules, never to switch the tool off. Logs must be sent to a central place, protected from change, and given synchronised clocks. Egress monitoring looks at what is leaving, and threat hunting assumes that someone is already inside. User and entity behaviour analytics spots an account doing something unusual, even when every action was technically allowed.

reviewSession.heading: Configuration and change: objectives 7.3 and 7.9
reviewSession.body: Let us take configuration and change management together, because people mix them up. Change management decides whether a change may happen. Configuration management records how things stand and checks that systems match. The baseline is the approved setup, and drift is moving away from it. If a weakness keeps appearing on new machines, fix the golden image and not each machine. The change steps are request, review, approve or reject, test, schedule and implement, and document. Every change needs a rollback plan. A change that worked but was never recorded still failed the process. In an emergency, a named person authorises the change, you act, and then you document and review it afterwards. The correct answer is rarely to do nothing, and rarely to skip the record. If a change has caused an outage, roll back first and ask questions later.

reviewSession.heading: Foundational concepts: objective 7.4
reviewSession.body: Now the foundations. Need to know is about information, and least privilege is about rights. Someone can have the right clearance and still have no need to know. Separation of duties means no one person completes a risky task alone, so fraud now needs collusion. It does not remove collusion. Job rotation and mandatory vacations reveal fraud that needs daily hiding, and rotation also gives cross-training. Privilege creep is what happens when old rights are kept, and access reviews are the cure. Shared administrator accounts destroy accountability, so the fix is individual accounts with recorded sessions. Be ready for a service level agreement calculation. At 99.9 percent of a 720 hour month, about 43 minutes of downtime is allowed. And remember the manager's view. You can hand over the work to a provider, but you never hand over accountability.

reviewSession.heading: Resource protection: objective 7.5
reviewSession.body: Let us move to resource protection. Deleting and formatting do not remove data. Learn clear, purge and destroy, from weakest to strongest. Clear defeats ordinary software tools. Purge defeats a laboratory, and it includes degaussing and cryptographic erase. Destroy means shredding, crushing or burning. The trap that catches people is that degaussing does not work on solid-state drives, so read the type of media carefully. If the data is very sensitive and the drive will not be reused, physical destruction is safest. Check for a legal hold before anything is destroyed, because a court case overrides the retention schedule. Encrypt anything that travels, send the key by another route, and treat a backup with the same care as the live data. Finally, match the control to the state of the data. Full-disk encryption protects data at rest on a powered-off device. It does nothing for data crossing a network.

reviewSession.heading: Incident management: objective 7.6
reviewSession.body: Incident management is one of the most heavily tested areas, so say the seven steps aloud with me. Detection. Response. Mitigation. Reporting. Recovery. Remediation. Lessons learned. When a question asks what comes next, work out which step has just been completed, and choose the very next one. People most often confuse recovery with remediation. Recovery brings the service back. Remediation removes the root cause, so the attacker cannot return the same way. Contain before you repair. Isolate a machine from the network, but leave it running, because memory holds evidence. Never hack back, since that may be illegal and may strike an innocent victim. Reporting has its own place in the list, but in practice it continues all the way through, and legal staff will know the time limits. Hold the lessons learned meeting last, and keep it free of blame.

reviewSession.heading: Detective and preventive measures: objective 7.7
reviewSession.body: Now let us revisit detective and preventive measures. A firewall list should end with implicit deny. A web application firewall reads web requests, and a next-generation firewall understands applications and users. Choose the tool that matches the attack in the question. An allow list blocks anything unknown, so it is stronger, and it suits stable systems. A deny list permits anything unknown, so it suits changing environments. A sandbox lets you watch what a file does, but a clean result is no guarantee. A honeypot must be isolated from real systems. Remember the legal line. Enticement leaves something available, and it is allowed. Entrapment persuades someone to commit a crime, and it is not allowed. Outside providers bring skills and hours, but accountability stays with you. Automated and learning tools help with scale, but people must still review what they produce.

reviewSession.heading: Patch and vulnerability management: objective 7.8
reviewSession.body: Next, patching and vulnerabilities. It all begins with an accurate inventory, because you cannot protect what you do not know about. A scan looks and reports, while a penetration test really tries to get in, and it needs written permission first. The name of a weakness comes from CVE, and its score comes from CVSS. Learn the bands. Low runs from 0.1 to 3.9, medium from 4.0 to 6.9, high from 7.0 to 8.9, and critical from 9.0 to 10.0. The trap is choosing the highest score. Look for facts about exposure, active attacks and business value, because risk decides the order. Test patches before production, send them through change management, and scan again to verify. If no patch exists, use compensating controls. If a system can never be patched, isolate it, and have management accept the remaining risk in writing.

reviewSession.heading: Recovery strategies: objective 7.10
reviewSession.body: Let us go back to recovery strategies, where exact details matter. Incremental backups copy what changed since the last backup of any kind, so a restore needs the full and every incremental in order. Differential backups copy what changed since the last full, so a restore needs the full and only the latest differential. Cold sites have space and power and take weeks. Warm sites have some equipment and older data and take days. Hot sites are fully equipped and take minutes or hours. Now the RAID levels. RAID 0 has two disks minimum and no fault tolerance. RAID 1 has two disks and survives one failure. RAID 5 has three disks and survives one failure. RAID 6 has four disks and survives two. RAID 10 has four disks and survives one failure in each mirrored pair. And RAID is never a backup.

reviewSession.heading: Disaster recovery and testing: objectives 7.11 and 7.12
reviewSession.body: Disaster recovery and its testing belong together. In a real event, people's safety comes first, and then a named person declares the disaster against clear triggers. Keep copies of the plan away from the main site and on paper. Plan several ways of communicating, and use one trained spokesperson. Now the direction of restoration, which people often reverse. Going to the recovery site, bring up the most critical work first. Coming home, move the least critical work first, to prove that the repaired site is stable. Test types run from least to most disruptive: read-through, tabletop, walkthrough, simulation, parallel and full interruption. A new plan starts with a read-through. If the question says the main site must keep running, a full interruption is ruled out. A parallel test gives real proof with no outage risk, and a full interruption needs senior management approval.

reviewSession.heading: Business continuity: objective 7.13
reviewSession.body: Now business continuity. It keeps the whole business working, while disaster recovery restores the technology. Your role on this objective is to participate and advise. The business owners and senior management decide what matters and accept the plan. Senior management support comes first, because without it there is no budget and no authority. The most tested rule is this. The recovery time objective plus the work recovery time must be no more than the maximum tolerable downtime. The recovery point objective is different. It looks backward, and it says how much data you can afford to lose. The trap is an answer that quietly changes a downtime figure so that a cheap option looks acceptable. The right answer is to explain the gap and let the business decide. In an exercise, follow the plan as written, and record every problem instead of quietly working around it.

reviewSession.heading: Physical security and personnel safety: objectives 7.14 and 7.15
reviewSession.body: Finally, physical security and the safety of people. Whenever a choice appears between protecting people and protecting things, people win. Exit doors fail safe, so that nobody is trapped. Fail-secure belongs on rooms where no one can be caught inside. Know the fence heights: three to four feet deters casual walkers, six to seven feet is hard to climb, and eight feet with three strands of barbed wire deters a determined intruder. Bollards stop vehicles, and an access control vestibule stops tailgating. Under duress, comply and raise the alarm silently. When travelling, take a clean device with only the data needed, and treat it with suspicion on return. Awareness training should cover insider threats, social media and repeated login prompts. Never approve a prompt that you did not start. That brings us to the end of this domain. Think like an adviser, put people first, and fix the cause.
